* fix(pack-1): use @example.com (RFC 2606) instead of @example.invalid (RFC 6761)

Pydantic v2 EmailStr rejects @example.invalid as a reserved/special-use TLD.
When pack 1's lite_playback_smoke seeds a user with @example.invalid and the
stitched candidate later does GET /admin/users, admin-api fails the
UserResponse validation and returns 500 for the entire endpoint, breaking
admin surfaces for every client.

@example.com is the RFC 2606 reserved-for-examples domain and parses cleanly.

* fix(pack-6): same-origin even with gatewayHostPort — bypass dashboard /ws rewrite breaks browser WS

Second stitched-candidate regression in the same pack 6 resolver. Compose
publishes dashboard on :41688 and gateway on :41680 as separate host ports.
The previous gatewayHostPort branch returned the direct gateway URL as
publicApiUrl, so /api/config emitted wsUrl=ws://localhost:41680/ws —
telling the browser to bypass the dashboard's /ws rewrite.

That works when the browser can reach BOTH host ports. It fails in any
single-port-exposed browser environment (sandboxes, dev-tunnel proxies,
some CI test browsers) with WS close code 1006. Curl-from-host still
worked, which is why the prior machine sweep missed it — same SSOT gap
between curl reachability and browser-context reachability.

The dashboard already has a /ws rewrite to ${VEXA_API_URL}/ws in
next.config.ts and a /api/vexa/[...path] proxy for REST. Both handle WS
upgrade correctly (verified HTTP 101 through dashboard :41688/ws). So
returning empty publicApiUrl lets the browser use same-origin and pipe
everything through the dashboard's existing rewrites.

Two root causes identified for "You can't join this meeting" on k8s
(Linode LKE datacenter IPs) that do NOT reproduce on compose (residential
or dev IPs):

1. Chrome fingerprint flags — baseBrowserArgs in constans.ts contained

  to the vexa-bot runtimeProfile so operators can route k8s bot pod

fix(security): gate /b/{token} browser-control routes — meeting_id alone must not grant access

The /b/{token}/cdp + /b/{token}/vnc|dashboard|save|storage routes were authenticated
ONLY by {token}, and meeting-api registered browser_session:{meeting_id} (a sequential
integer). Anyone who guessed the integer could connectOverCDP to a live bot's browser
(read the meeting, drive the page) or open its VNC — no API key. Account-crossing
browser takeover.

Two gates, by surface:
- CDP (programmatic): api-gateway now requires X-API-Key whose user OWNS the session
  (_authorize_browser_token), on both the HTTP and WS paths. meeting_id stays usable
  here because the api-key+ownership is the real gate.
- VNC / dashboard / save / storage (browser-opened, cannot carry a header): gated by an
  UNGUESSABLE capability token in the URL. The gateway rejects numeric (meeting_id)
  tokens on these routes; meeting-api escalation now issues secrets.token_urlsafe(24)
  instead of str(meeting.id) for the VNC URL.

Verified live: meeting_id -> 403 on all browser-opened routes + CDP-without-key; owner
key -> 200 on CDP; secret capability token -> 200 on VNC.

Regression locks: CDP_ATTACH_REQUIRES_OWNER_TOKEN, VNC_REJECTS_GUESSABLE_TOKEN,
ESCALATION_USES_SECRET_TOKEN (+ the 4 bot-functionality locks).

fix(mixed-pipeline): despeckle pyannote class wobbles → stop oversegmentation

On a continuous single speaker, pyannote's powerset briefly flickers into an overlap/other-speaker class; handleBoundary hard-splits on those → the turn shatters into seg_N fragments AND Whisper's window breaks at the cut (so post-hoc text merge can't recover it). Live result on a council-meeting recording: ≤3-word fragments 36%→0%, segments now coherent 20-60-word paragraphs, no lost transcripts. Goldens unaffected (they inject a fake segmenter). VEXA_SEG_DEBUG gates a split-boundary + class-context log.

fix(eval): lane-aware capture health — stop mis-diagnosing gmeet

The capture probe judged every tape on ch999 + ch1000 and discarded per-participant
channels (idx != 999/1000) as 'other'. For Google Meet — whose remote audio rides
PER-PARTICIPANT channels 0..N — it could never see the real feed and always cried
'ch999 absent → tab-capture not minted (Zoom/Teams symptom)'. That's the false alarm
that made a solo gmeet tape read UNHEALTHY.

  - classify channels: [0,998]=gmeet participant · 999=mixed-remote · 1000=mic · >1000=REC1 chunk.
  - branch health on the tape's platform: mixed→ch999; gmeet→per-participant ch0..N.
  - 3-state verdict (healthy·inconclusive·unhealthy): a gmeet tape with only the mic is

fix(0.12): CC5 — a workload that dies before the bot reports drives the meeting to `failed`

lifecycle event (image-pull fail, OOM, crash on boot) left the meeting stuck `requested`/`joining`
forever — misleadingly pending, no terminal webhook. (The code comment flagged this as a follow-up; the
live bbb logs showed a real `runtime_callback state:destroyed` ACKed-only.)

Fix: on a TERMINAL workload state while the meeting is still PRE-ACTIVE, the runtime callback drives a
synthetic `failed` (failure_stage = the stage it died in) through the bot's OWN lifecycle callback
(POST-to-self → identical FSM/persist/webhook/ws path). Scoped to pre-active to avoid racing a legit
completion; active/terminal meetings are no-ops (owned by the bot's callback). New repo lookup
`find_by_container` (real + fake); the decision is the importable, testable
`lifecycle/reconcile.synthesize_failed_for_dead_workload`.

The all-in-one desktop is the cloud collector's counterpart. Its in-memory store
appended every confirmed segment (Array.push), so a late-box claim / cluster
re-resolve that re-publishes the SAME segment_id with the corrected speaker left

fix(dashboard_new): zoom join sends meeting_url + recording seek aligns to the recording origin

Two dashboard fixes:

1. Zoom 422 — POST /bots for zoom returned 422 "unsupported platform 'zoom' without a meeting_url".
   The zoom branch of parseMeetingInput omitted `originalUrl` (the Teams branch sets it), so JoinForm
   never populated `meeting_url`, which the backend REQUIRES for zoom (the join needs the full link +
   pwd, not just the numeric id). The zoom branch now preserves the original URL like Teams does.

2. Recording-seek alignment — clicking a transcript utterance landed early by the lead-in silence.
   The seek anchored playback t=0 to `min(segment start_times)` = the first UTTERANCE, and was
   incoherent for the epoch-scale `start_time` live segments carry. It now derives the recording ORIGIN
   in wall-clock (origin = absolute_start_time − relative start_time, the earliest such anchor — the old
   dashboard's `sessionStart = absolute − start_time`) and seeks by the absolute delta from that origin.
   Consistent for REST (relative) and live (epoch) start_times; anchored to the recording's real start.

fix(bot): stamp canonical absolute_start_time at the producer (kill the 2082 timestamp)

Transcript segments showed absolute_start_time in the YEAR 2082, scrambling recording-seek + transcript
ordering. Root cause: the lanes emit `start`/`end` as EPOCH seconds (windowStartMs/1000), but they left
absolute_start_time empty — so the meeting-api transcript read derived it as `meeting_start + start`,
treating an epoch (~1.78e9 s ≈ 56 years) as a relative offset → 2026 + 56y = 2082.

We own the producer, so emit the truth once instead of re-deriving (and guessing units) downstream:
toBotSegment — the single chokepoint every lane's segment passes through, where `start` is known to be
epoch seconds — now stamps absolute_start_time/absolute_end_time = ISO(start). The dashboard renderer
and the meeting-api read both consume it directly; no consumer re-derives from `start`. Regression test
asserts absolute_start_time == epoch(start). (Read-side heuristic reverted — the producer is authoritative.)

fix(agent-api): the chat SSE-view closes on turn-complete, reads from $ (M1)

RedisStreamReader was terminating on `done`, which the worker emits BEFORE `commit` — so the terminal
never saw the commit. Close the relay on `turn-complete` (the worker's terminal marker, after
done+commit) instead, and read from $ so a later turn never replays a prior turn's stream.

fix(agent): save + resume chats FROM THE WORKSPACE (durable chat memory)

Chat had no memory across turns: each chat message recreates the worker container, and claude-code
keeps a conversation's transcript in the container's ephemeral ~/.claude/projects — wiped each turn —
so --resume had nothing to restore, and the agent also wrote 'memory' to ~/.claude (lost on recreate).

- worker._link_chat_into_workspace: symlink ~/.claude/projects -> <workspace>/.claude/projects, so
  claude writes the conversation transcript INTO the durable git workspace and --resume reads it back
  across container recreations. Kept under .claude (excluded from the governance git clean) so a
  rejected turn never wipes history; persists on the workspace volume.
- worker seed CLAUDE.md: explicitly tell the agent the workspace (cwd) is its ONLY durable memory —
  save knowledge as files here, never to ~/.claude.

feat(bot): make segment-latency knobs env-configurable (#447)

SpeakerStreamManager hardcodes three timing constants tuned for
transcription quality (longer buffers = more STT context):

  minAudioDuration: 3   submitInterval: 2   idleTimeoutSec: 15

This makes Vexa unusable for real-time / voice-agent use: a short
utterance (~2s) never reaches the 3s minAudioDuration, so it falls
through to the 15s idle timeout before being sent to the transcription
service — the caller sees the transcript ~15s after the speaker stops.

Make the three knobs env-overridable while keeping the existing
defaults (behavior unchanged unless opted into), mirroring the
existing MAX_SPEECH_DURATION_SEC / MIN_SILENCE_DURATION_MS overrides:

profiles.yaml plumbs them through to the meeting bot container, so a
deployment can opt into low-latency mode, e.g.:

  MIN_AUDIO_DURATION_SEC=0.5 SUBMIT_INTERVAL_SEC=1 IDLE_TIMEOUT_SEC=1.5

dropping end-of-speech latency from ~15s to ~2s for short utterances.

fix(meeting-api): offload blocking boto3 S3 calls off the event loop (#458)

Several async handlers in meeting-api call the synchronous boto3 storage
client directly on the asyncio event loop. The hot path is the recording
chunk upload (one put_object per chunk), so under concurrent recording
load these blocking network calls serialize on the single loop thread and
stall it for seconds — long enough for the trivial liveness/readiness
probes to time out and Kubernetes to restart the pod, even though it is
not CPU- or memory-bound.

Wrap every synchronous storage call made from async code in
asyncio.to_thread(...), matching the pattern already used in
recording_finalizer.py:

- recordings.py: chunk upload (upload_file), master file_exists /
  get_presigned_url, and raw download_file
- meetings.py: audio download_file
- sweeps.py: list_objects_bounded (both sweep paths)

boto3 clients are thread-safe across distinct operations, so this is a
behaviour-preserving change that simply unblocks the loop. Add a
regression test asserting the chunk upload executes on a worker thread
rather than the event-loop thread.

fix(meeting-api): treat max_concurrent_bots=0 as depleted, not unlimited (#456)

Both per-user concurrency gates only entered the check when the limit was > 0,
so max_concurrent_bots=0 fell straight through and granted UNLIMITED concurrent
bots — a quota/billing bypass. 0 is meant to mean "depleted" (the dashboard
renders it that way) and is the admin-api default for new users, so the
most-restricted users were effectively unlimited (#402).

Extract the duplicated gate into _enforce_bot_concurrency_limit() and treat a
limit of <= 0 as depleted (HTTP 403). Unlimited access is represented by a large
positive limit (e.g. dev mode's 999), never 0.

- meetings.py: shared _enforce_bot_concurrency_limit helper (0 = depleted),
  used by both the browser_session and request_bot gates (the latter still
  excludes browser_session meetings from the active count)
- tests: depleted (0) -> 403, under-limit -> allowed, at-limit -> 403

Stage 5 (cookbook #1): chat grounding via a meeting-scoped tool

The chat agent learns a live meeting's transcript through an authorized,
meeting-scoped TOOL — meetings' published /transcripts contract — not a file
(P23/P3). tools-seed/meeting-read-transcript.json (tool.v1, validated on load)
declares an auto MCP grant targeting /transcripts. api.chat() grounds on the
terminal's active meeting via _meeting_grounding(): meeting context + the tool +
a 'you are in a live meeting' preamble, only when active.kind==meeting. The
dispatcher already mints the token scoped to invocation.tools (dispatch.py:119);
dispatch now also injects VEXA_MEETING_NATIVE_ID/PLATFORM so the tool can target
the meeting. CP6 deterministic plumbing tests added.

warrants, scoped to one resource. Deferred behind the wired seam (P16): the live

Stage 6 (cookbook #2): 'agent on a meeting' composed op

meetingCookbook.agentOnMeeting() composes the two PUBLISHED domain contracts —
meetings POST /bots + agent POST /api/meeting/process — into one state-delivering
call, ABOVE both domains (composition never lives inside a domain). send bot ≠
start copilot (two toggles, two domains) folded into one op. Partial failure of
the agent step is SURFACED in the combined state (the bot is already in); a hard
meetings-step failure throws (P18). CP8 deterministic test (4 cases) green;
terminal surfaces suite green (64).

Cookbook composition pattern #2. The reusable seam is delivered + tested; binding
it to a specific UI control is a thin client integration (left to product, since
the two toggles stay independently available).

Stage 7 (CP5, lighter): document the live-view composition seam

Post-D7 the live SSE reads the meetings-owned transcript carrier + composes the
agent's cards — a reader composing, not a P23 violation — so the gateway-compose
relocation is a user-invisible follow-up, not a fix. Document CP5's current home
(agent-api SSE) + deferred gateway move; the merge + gapless dual-stream cursor
are already pinned by _encode/_decode_sse_cursor + test_meeting_stream. Add a
'Deferred (seam wired, impl follows — P16)' section to CONTROL-PLANE.md.

Refine SoC principle: legal acquisition, not 'never touch'

The boundary is write-ownership + how data is acquired, not forbidding
possession. The agent MAY hold/compose/serve meeting data downstream once
acquired LEGALLY through a published contract (gateway /transcripts, or the
transcript.v1 carrier). Forbidden: owning/writing another domain's carrier,
re-deriving a producer's data (P23), or reaching into internals (P3). Corrects
the Stage-7 'soft bleed' framing — the agent's live-view composition + chat tool
both legally acquire the transcript, then use their own downstream copy. Update
agent README boundary + CONTROL-PLANE.md §1.

fix(agent): scrub GIT_DIR from git subprocess env — pre-push hook was rewriting the pushed branch

Git exports GIT_DIR (and sometimes GIT_WORK_TREE / GIT_INDEX_FILE) into hook
processes. .githooks/pre-push runs `pnpm gates`; gate:python runs core/agent's
pytest suite; and every workspace git subprocess in it (seeding, attach,
adapters, the harness turn commit, the tests' own git helpers) inherited that
env. With GIT_DIR pointing at the real repo and no work tree given, git treats
the subprocess's tmp cwd as the REAL repo's work tree — so each test's
`git add -A && git commit` rewrote the branch being pushed. This destroyed
feat/webhook-parity (~180 junk commits deleting the tree) and transiently
corrupted feat/mcp-service.

The fix, two layers:

* Library (the real fix): core/agent/shared/gitenv.py provides
  scrubbed_git_env() — os.environ minus every var that redirects git's repo
  discovery (GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, GIT_INDEX_FILE, GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY,
  GIT_COMMON_DIR, GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES; GIT_AUTHOR_* /
  GIT_COMMITTER_* / GIT_CONFIG_* are deliberately kept). Every git call site
  routes through it: shared/seeding.py (seed init/add/commit),
  shared/adapters.py (_git + RealGitWorkspace.clone),
  control_plane/workspace_attach.py (_git_clone, _git_commit_all),
  control_plane/workspace_reader.py (git_state). llm/ports.py carries a
  module-local twin (the llm module imports nothing from product code) used
  by its _git and by the harness CLI launchers (claude_cli.py,
  claude_code.py) — the harness itself shells out to git in the workspace.
  tests/conftest.py drops the vars from os.environ at session import so the
  tests' own subprocess git helpers are covered wholesale.

* Hook (belt and braces): .githooks/pre-push unsets the same vars before
  running the gates.

Regression test: tests/test_gitdir_scrub.py builds a scratch "victim" repo
with one commit, sets GIT_DIR at its .git, runs seed_workspace and
run_harness_turn's commit path in a separate tmp dir, and asserts the
victim's HEAD/branch/tree are untouched while the helper committed to its
own directory. Verified to fail on the unfixed code (the victim's HEAD is
rewritten — the incident in miniature) and pass with the fix. Full suite:
252 passed; gates readme / python / isolation-py / graph-py green.

Signed-off-by: Dmitry Grankin <dmitry@vexa.ai>

fix(runtime): wire RUNTIME_STOP_GRACE_SEC into the kernel stop-poll window

The backends terminate() honoured the env, but Runtime.stop() polled for its
own grace_sec — stuck at the 5.0 constructor default because
build_production_app never set it. On k8s (terminate returns immediately with
--wait=false; the pod phase stays Running through graceful deletion) the kernel
force-killed at t=5: the 30s grace and the bot leave watchdog were dead
letters. Docker was unaffected only because its terminate() blocks.

_kernel_grace_sec derives the kernel window from the SAME env (default 30) plus
a 5s margin, so the kernel force-kill lands strictly AFTER the substrate grace
elapses. Declares RUNTIME_STOP_GRACE_SEC in config.v1 (the #49 gate requires
every env read declared — the exact entry the #49 review pre-verified).

fix(meeting-api): bound the untracked-workload loop — escalate to failed with evidence

"Untracked, never reap" is right as a reflex (a recreated runtime forgets live
bots — amnesia is not evidence) but wrong as a steady state: on the process
backend the workers die WITH the runtime (adopt() is a no-op, no callback will
ever come), so every meeting live across a runtime restart looped
meeting_workload_untracked at error level + a dead DELETE every 15s, forever.
k8s pod GC/eviction produces the same dead end routinely.

The general sweep now tracks CONTINUOUS untracked observations per meeting;
once one spans MEETING_UNTRACKED_GRACE_SEC (default 600) with no recovery — no
runtime re-adoption, no bot callback — the meeting advances to failed through
the bot lifecycle callback, carrying the evidence note ("workload untracked
for >Ns; presumed lost — runtime restart or external removal") at WARN, and
the loop converges (the terminal row leaves the listing). Any sign of life
resets the window: a probe answering alive/gone, or a row leaving the stale
listing (bot callback/heartbeat bumped it). The tracker is in-process by
design — a meeting-api restart only ever DELAYS an escalation, never
fabricates one. Covers the stopping/pre-active teardown-404 path too via the
same window.

fix(terminal): chat stream survives worker cold-start — resume, don't show false failure

A fresh user's first chat message spawns a FRESH per-dispatch agent worker (docker
backend) that takes several seconds to boot. The chat SSE gave up the moment the
stream closed early and rendered "No chat output arrived before the stream
closed" — a FALSE failure: the turn is never lost (the worker completes, commits,
and saves the session .jsonl; the reply is there on reopen).

Root cause: the chat SSE path had no resume contract. The client's reader loop
declared failure on any early close (cold-start window / transient proxy drop),
and the backend chat stream neither emitted resumable id: cursors nor accepted
Last-Event-ID (unlike /api/meeting/stream, which already resumes gaplessly).

  Stream id instead of "$"; yield (event, cursor) so the SSE emits id: lines.
- POST /api/chat surfaces those cursors and, on a reconnect (Last-Event-ID
  present), RE-ATTACHES to the deterministic warm unit and resumes from the
  cursor WITHOUT dispatching a second turn.
- StreamReader port + fakes updated; 2 new resume tests (resumable ids; resume
  re-attaches with no second dispatch). Agent suite 281 green.

  reconnects with Last-Event-ID on an early close, distinguishes "still

request is abandoned even where no cancel is reachable (Meet lobby / Zoom). Active

hours. The worker only reaps on a session_end marker on tc:meeting:{native} or its

TERMINAL FSM advance emit the session_end marker onto tc:meeting:{native} — the
exact feed the copilot blocks on — so it reaps immediately regardless of how the

feat(chat): verbose live status + recover a stalled SSE (no more silent stale)

The chat could look frozen with no clue why. Two causes, both fixed:

- A STALLED stream (SSE open but sending nothing — dead proxy/gateway, half-open
  TCP) blocked reader.read() forever; the resume loop only fired on a CLOSE, so it
  hung until the 90s hard cap. Now each read races an idle deadline: no bytes for
  ~18s ⇒ cancel + reconnect from the Last-Event-ID cursor (same warm unit, no
  duplicate dispatch). chatStream.readOrStall.
- No feedback between events. Added a live phase — connecting / working /
  reconnecting / stalled — with a heartbeat every ~3.5s and a self-ticking
  elapsed-seconds status line (agent-window StatusLine), so a long think / tool run /
  reconnect reads as ALIVE. `since` is per-gap so the counter shows the CURRENT wait.
  Replaces the old "_Starting agent…_" text hack.

- Non-OK responses are split: 4xx = a real client/terminal error (surfaced, no

- If a turn genuinely can't recover past the hard cap, the pane now says so even with

fix(agent+terminal): chat SSE 'Reconnecting' hang — pre-dispatch tail attach + turn-nonce retry + keepalives

Incident (user 28): turns hung at 'Reconnecting · Ns' while the worker ran/finished.
(A) the chat reader attached at $ AFTER dispatch, so events written in the
dispatch→attach gap — or a whole turn finishing during a reconnect gap — were
invisible forever to a client that never got a cursor. Fresh turns now snapshot
the out-Stream tail BEFORE dispatching and attach there ('stream START' was
unsafe: the thread stream holds prior turns and the client stops on any

retry re-attaches from the turn's recorded start with NO second dispatch.

streams ~18-30s into a long think: the reader now yields an idle tick every
block_ms (15s) that _sse emits as an SSE ': keepalive' comment; idle giveup
raised to 10min since bytes now flow.

agent: warm delivery — fix the lost-turn touch race + turn-accepted liveness ack

The runtime's create is an idempotent TOUCH for a running workload (ADR-0027):
it returns the live status and discards the spec env — where a chat message's
prompt rides. Nothing wrote the prompt to unit:<id>:in, so a message sent while
the thread's worker was alive (mid-turn or parked in its serve() idle window)
dispatched NOWHERE: the UI hung on 'Starting agent' until the worker idled out
(<=120s — the observed 109s hangs). The worker's warm serve loop was dead code
for chat.

- dispatcher pre-delivers message-trigger prompts to unit:<id>:in BEFORE the
  spawn call: a warm worker consumes them (fast path — no container/CLI cold
  start); a cold spawn skips the pre-delivered copy via serve()'s new
  boot-time in-topic tail anchor and runs the same prompt as its entrypoint.
- delivery watchdog: no turn-accepted ack + workload gone => one respawn
  (closes the XADD <-> idle-exit race).
- worker emits turn-accepted at every turn pickup (echoing the delivery
  nonce) — the UI flips off 'Starting agent' in ms, and a silent
  failure-to-start becomes observable.
- chat idle window configurable (VEXA_CHAT_IDLE_TIMEOUT_SEC, default 900s)
  so follow-ups land warm; declared in config.v1.json.
- terminal: turn-accepted flips the heartbeat to 'working'.

runtime: enforce workspace tenant isolation on all three backends

Workers previously received the WHOLE workspace store read-write (docker bind /
k8s PVC mounted at the root; lite children share the FS outright) — any agent
could read or write any tenant's workspace; the three-tier mount stack was a
prompt-level convention, not a boundary. Now isolation is enforced by the
substrate, default-on (VEXA_WORKSPACE_ISOLATION=strict; legacy = the old
whole-store exposure, the escape hatch for docker engines < v26):

- docker: one bind PER MOUNT — a named-volume store rides the Mounts API's
  VolumeOptions.Subpath, a host-path store joins the subpath; read-only roles
  bind :ro (enforced, not just the commit token). The container's filesystem
  contains ONLY the dispatch's declared mount set.
- k8s: per-mount subPath + readOnly volumeMounts against the one store PVC
  (native, no version caveat). Helm exposes runtime.workspaceIsolation.
- lite/process: POSIX enforcement (new runtime_kernel/isolation.py) — workers
  drop to a per-subject uid (100000+id), private/system tiers 0700-owned,
  shared workspaces get per-workspace gids (persisted registry) joined as
  supplementary groups, per-subject HOME/TMPDIR, and a default-deny sweep
  seals never-dispatched tenants' dirs. Unavailable conditions (non-root,
  non-numeric subject) degrade LOUDLY to shared-trust.

One change carrying several values rides one issue with a value sentence + acceptance
row + preferred validator PER value; values needing different changes never bundle —
relatedness is a same-setup board note. Two-way test at preparation review; template
note + compliance row (row-per-value check folds into the bundle checker TO BUILD).

D6c: the docs are part of the change; the docs STORY is part of the human validation

A change isn't delivered until the documentation tells it — usually in several
places at several altitudes (quickstart / how-to / reference / concept), each
written for its reader. Prepared issues name their docs surface before ready;
the PR carries the docs diff beside the code diff; the validator's attestation
covers the docs story — right pages, right level, consistent with how the docs
already teach. Diátaxis as the altitude vocabulary.

D12b: every validation names its deployment; setup build provenance is evidence

A behavior proven on one deployment is proven on that one. Prepared issues
declare which deployments the acceptance table runs against (Lite called out
deliberately — most divergent path, may need its own run); every attestation
names its setup AND how it was built (sha, compose/values, fresh-clone vs
long-lived, env deltas) — the D10 anchor rule applied to the environment.

gateway: port fastapi-guard edge layer to 0.12 — per-IP throttle + auto-ban + static blocklist (closes #544) (#555)

* feat(gateway): port fastapi-guard edge layer to 0.12 gateway (edge_guard.py)

Ports the 0.10.7 guard_config.py to the 0.12 gateway as edge_guard.py:
per-IP rate limiting + auto-IP-ban at the edge, complementary to the
per-user rate limiter (per-key catches one-token-many-IPs; per-IP catches
many-tokens-from-one-IP + auto-bans repeat offenders).

- edge_guard.py: build_guard_config()/apply_guard() ported verbatim from
  0.10.7 (fail_secure=False, lazy_init=True, request-body WAF OFF, CORS OFF,
  security-headers OFF). exclude_paths adds /health. Optional WS guard hook
  (GUARD_WS_ENABLED, default false) — standalone in-memory limiter since
  SecurityMiddleware exposes no reusable programmatic IP-check (dispatch is
  HTTP-Request-bound); shares vexa:guard: namespace, not the HTTP middleware's
  in-process counters.
- adapters.build_production_app: apply_guard(app) on the create_app result
  (prod-only; create_app stays pure so the conformance harness is unaffected).
- app.run_multiplex: WS guard hook right after ws.accept(), gated by
  GUARD_WS_ENABLED (default false → WS path unchanged).
- pyproject.toml: fastapi-guard>=7.2,<8.0; uv.lock regenerated.
- tests/test_edge_guard.py: 3 wiring + 3 behavior + 3 WS-hook tests.
- conftest.py: GUARD_ENABLED=true, GUARD_ENABLE_REDIS=false,
  GUARD_RATE_LIMIT_RPM=0 (installed but inert for the existing suite).
- Deploy surfaces (compose, helm, lite, .env.example): GUARD_ENABLED=false +
  GUARD_WS_ENABLED=false (self-hosted default OFF; hosted enables via env;
  code default ON for deployments that set no value).
- README Status line updated.

* fix(gateway/edge_guard): D1-D3 + P1 corrections from adversarial review

D1: WS XFF resolution now matches guard_core's HTTP path — keys on the
rightmost XFF entry (ips[-trusted_proxy_depth], default depth=1) when the
peer is trusted, and ignores XFF entirely when the peer is untrusted (so a
spoofed XFF from an untrusted source cannot rotate the WS rate-limit/ban
budget). The prior leftmost-entry selection was the most attacker-spoofable
position. Docstring corrected (was falsely claiming parity with guard_core).

D2: Disclosed the in-memory per-process WS-guard ceiling on every
operator-facing surface (README, docker-compose, .env.example, helm
deployment, lite supervisord) — the /ws guard does NOT share ban/rate-limit
state with the Redis-backed HTTP SecurityMiddleware, and under
uvicorn --workers N>1 each worker keeps an independent WS ban set.
Default OFF; opt-in via GUARD_WS_ENABLED.

D3: Added the 3 missing acceptance-floor tests:
  - A2: auto-ban persists past the rate-window reset (drive over the
    auto_ban_threshold, assert the next request is still banned after the
    rate window resets but within the ban window). Uses a fake clock.
  - A5: both layers in one app — valid-key burst → per-user 429
    (rate_limiter, Retry-After: 1) and keyless flood → per-IP 429 (guard,
    no Retry-After), proving the two 429 paths coexist.
  - A4 spoofed-XFF: untrusted peer's XFF does NOT rotate the WS budget.
Also made _enforcing_config accept an auto-ban-enabling variant
(enable_ip_banning=True + small auto_ban_threshold/auto_ban_duration).

P1: Reset ban_counts and the rate bucket when a ban is SET, so after the
ban window expires the offender starts a fresh cycle (a single over-limit
does NOT immediately re-ban — a fresh threshold's worth is required). The
A2 test covers this: after ban expiry, one over-limit returns ip_blocked
(rate) but the next window-reset connect passes (not re-banned).

Also gated the auto-ban path on cfg.enable_ip_banning — the config field
was being ignored, so banning could slip in via the back door even when
an operator set enable_ip_banning=False.

P2 (WS deny before ws.accept): deferred — moving the check before accept
would drop the ip_blocked error frame (send_text cannot run pre-accept)
and is an opt-in toggle defaulting OFF, not load-bearing.

Gates: ruff check + format clean on both files; mypy clean on edge_guard.py
(the 2 reported app.py errors are pre-existing and out of scope); bandit
clean (0 issues); full gateway pytest 57 passed, 1 xfailed.

* fix(gateway/edge_guard): bare '/' in exclude_paths neutered the whole guard layer

Live image testing (A9) found guard's per-IP rate limit never fired
on the booted production gateway — no 429, no redis keys, empty
in-memory counters. Root cause: guard matches exclude_paths with
url_path.startswith(path) (prefix, not exact), and _GUARD_EXCLUDE_PATHS
contained a bare "/", which matches EVERY path (all start with "/"),
so is_path_excluded short-circuited the entire security pipeline on
every route. The guard layer was a silent no-op in production.

The unit suite missed it: TestGuardBehavior used _enforcing_config
(exclude_paths=[]), and TestGuardWiring only hit /health (excluded
correctly) — no test flooded a guarded path with the REAL shipped
exclude list.

Fix: drop "/" from _GUARD_EXCLUDE_PATHS. The root landing is a cheap
route; an IP spending its per-minute budget on it is harmless, and
prefix-matching makes excluding exactly "/" impossible anyway. Add a
regression test (test_real_exclude_paths_do_not_neuter_guard) that
floods / with the real exclude list + rate_limit=3 and asserts a 429,
plus an explicit 'assert "/" not in _GUARD_EXCLUDE_PATHS' guard.

Verified live: rebuilt image, flooded /bots x6 redis-backed → 429 on
req4-6 with key vexa:guard:rate_limit:rate:<ip> written; redis-stop →
fail-open (401, not 500), /health stays 200. Gates: 13 passed (was 12),
ruff/format/mypy(edge_guard)/bandit clean.

- errors.mdx: rewrite 'Rate limits' — two layers (per-IP pre-auth edge throttle, per-user post-auth
  limiter), 429 + Retry-After, auto-ban semantics; fixes the stale 'no gateway rate limit' claim
  (the per-user limiter is on by default); add 429 to the status-codes table.
- configuration.mdx: new 'Gateway edge protection' section — the GATEWAY_RATE_LIMIT_* per-user knobs
  (previously undocumented) + the full GUARD_* surface, defaults, and the GUARD_ENABLED kill switch.
- deployment.mdx: reverse-proxy section gains the GUARD_TRUSTED_PROXIES + X-Forwarded-For step and
  the why (without it, per-IP keys collapse to the proxy IP — one bucket for everyone).
- security-compliance.mdx: the 'one front door' posture bullet gains the edge-abuse layer, its
  self-hosted default (OFF), and the kill switch.

* fix(deploy): wire GUARD_* env end-to-end — ON by default with generous limits (owner ruling)

Maintainer fix-forward on #555. The guard shipped dark and unswitchable:

- compose: literal GUARD_ENABLED=false ignored .env entirely (compose does

- lite: supervisord literal GUARD_ENABLED="false" overrode container env ->

GUARD_WS_ENABLED stays default false (opt-in by design).

The gateway used ONE httpx.AsyncClient (pool cap 10, 30s timeout) for both
jobs: forwarding to meeting-api AND validating API keys against admin-api.
When meeting-api slowed, forwards saturated the shared pool, the ~5ms
validation POST queued and timed out, resolve() swallowed the exception and
returned None, and the app rendered that as `401 Invalid API key` — mass-401ing

   `auth_infra_unavailable` log line replaces the old silent `except` (FM02).

meeting-api: pipeline liveness observable + bounded stream retention (#527) (#606)

On 2026-04-26 the persistence consumer froze inside one await for 10h38m. /health
kept returning 200, the k8s liveness probe kept passing, and live WS transcripts
kept flowing (a SEPARATE code path) — so everything looked alive while zero rows
reached the DB. Discovery was a user opening an empty transcript; 20 meetings'
transcripts were permanently lost because the stream's MAXLEN trim aged entries
out before recovery. The diagnostic signal (XINFO CONSUMERS idle/lag) existed the
whole time, read by nobody and exposed nowhere.

C1 — liveness observable. Each background loop stamps a monotonic heartbeat on
app.state after every iteration; a loop hung inside an await stops stamping. GET
/health gains an ADDITIVE `pipeline` section (per-loop tick_age_s + collector-group
lag via a 2s-bounded XINFO) that flips status→degraded + 503 on a stale loop or
lag over PIPELINE_LAG_ALARM. The section appears ONLY when the loops are wired
(build_production_app sets app.state.pipeline_ticks); the bare app-factory path
(unit/conformance) is byte-unchanged — status ok, no section — so existing /health
consumers keep working. The probe is itself bounded (wait_for 2s → "unavailable")
so observing a hung pipeline can never hang the request.

C2 — bounded retention that never loses unread data. db_writer_tick trims
transcription_segments to entries newer than STREAM_RETENTION_S, but never past an
un-consumed entry: the floor is the OLDER of {retention time, oldest PENDING
(delivered-unacked), last-delivered-id + 1 (the UNDELIVERED lag)}. An acked-and-aged
entry is trimmed; a pending or undelivered entry always survives (the 04-26
data-loss guard). A behind/hung group keeps its full backlog — the hang is now
caught by C1, not papered over by trimming its unread entries. No group/stream yet
→ no blind trim.

Knobs (PIPELINE_TICK_STALE_S, PIPELINE_LAG_ALARM, STREAM_RETENTION_S) declared in
config.v1.json (config-contract gate green). Tests: test_pipeline_health (bare→ok
no-section; healthy→ok+section; stale loop→503; high lag→503; probe fail→
unavailable-not-hang) and test_stream_retention (acked-aged trimmed; pending kept;
undelivered kept; no-group→no blind trim) via fakeredis. meeting-api lane 642
passed / 2 skipped.

db-budget: CI gate auditing Σ(replicas × pool ceiling) vs max_connections (#529) (#610)

On 2026-04-21 the hosted deploy spent ~3h partially down — dashboard 500s, sign-in
"Access Denied" — because the sum of per-service DB pool ceilings exceeded the
managed Postgres max_connections (100). Every service held its ceiling privately;
no layer knew the sum; the first signal was user-facing TooManyConnectionsError.
The post-state margin ("~72 of 100") lived only as hand-arithmetic in a postmortem
table — nowhere in code or CI.

Add gate:db-budget (the accounting, now enforced):
- deploy/db-budget.json declares max_connections, a reserved headroom, and per
  DB-holding service {helm_key, pool_size, max_overflow}. The 0.12 tree has exactly
  two Postgres services — admin-api and meeting-api — each at the SQLAlchemy
  framework default (pool 5 + overflow 10 = 15); agent-api/runtime/gateway are
  Redis-only.
- scripts/gates.mjs gateDbBudget(): reads each service's replicaCount from helm
  values.yaml, computes Σ(replicas × ceiling) + reserved, and FAILS if it exceeds
  max_connections — printing the per-service breakdown (the postmortem table).
  Σ = admin-api(2×15) + meeting-api(2×15) + 10 = 70/100 — the same safe margin the
  postmortem maintained by hand, now a green check.
- Two drift guards: (1) any service whose non-test source constructs a
  create_async_engine but is absent from the budget fails the gate (a new
  DB-holding service can't slip in unaccounted); (2) a budget that under-states an
  explicit pool_size/max_overflow the code sets fails (can't be gamed).
- Wired into CI (package.json + gates.yml) beside gate:config-contract.

Proven: green at Σ 70/100; RED when max_connections is lowered below Σ (exact
arithmetic shown), RED when a DB service is dropped from the budget (named). Note:
this is the DIRECT-connection worst case (pgbouncer off); pgbouncer transaction-mode
decouples per-pod pools from server slots.

fix(recordings): per-chunk durable upload + finalize-on-read (#509, #491, #412) (#611)

Two paying-user defects, both about the same promise — the audio you recorded is
the audio you can get back:

  #491: bot logs show 201 uploads and has_recording:true, but /recordings serves
        the empty final-signal chunk (0 bytes) — confirmed uploads are unretrievable.
  #412: a long meeting's older audio parts are lost — the whole recording was held
        in Node memory and one master uploaded at graceful close, so a crash loses
        everything and only the last file survives.

Three surgical seams:

C2 (meeting-api, load-bearing — retrieval serves the whole recording, never the
    signal chunk):
  - router.py get_recording_media_raw: stop trusting media-file `is_final` as
    "storage_path is playable". Always finalize-on-read into the assembled master
    unless storage_path is already a master.<fmt> key, then re-read. After an
    empty-final fold storage_path named the zero-byte signal object -> /raw served
    0 bytes (#491); is_final no longer doubles as "playable".
  - jsonb.py apply_chunk_to_recording: never let media_files.storage_path name an
    empty signal chunk — when file_size==0 and a prior media-file of this type
    exists, keep the prior storage_path (the master is assembled from all chunks on
    read).
  Result: a confirmed upload downloads byte-complete via GET /recordings/{id}/master
  AND …/media/{id}/raw, for every recording the list shows.

C1 (bot — every part durable the moment it is recorded):
  - recording.ts createBotRecordingSink: stop accumulating into
    createRecordingAssembler + uploading one master at close. Each MediaRecorder
    timeslice now uploads immediately via RecordingService.uploadChunk (already
    shipped with retry/backoff at recording.ts:222, zero production callers before
    this), serialized in seq order; a permanently-failed chunk is logged-and-skipped.
    session_uid == inv.connectionId (the eager-created MeetingSession the server
    resolves against). The empty is_final chunk is forwarded (COMPLETED signal);
    close(key) is the final-signal FALLBACK — one empty is_final if the live Stop
    race dropped the tap's own final, fired at most once. A SIGKILL now leaves every
    finished part durable; the master is assembled server-side on first /master|/raw.
  - capture-bridge.ts startRecording: the MediaRecorder timeslice (= durable-upload
    granularity) is env-overridable via VEXA_RECORDING_TIMESLICE_MS (default 15000),
    the knob a live multi-part run uses. The assembler stays in @vexa/recording
    (desktop still uses it); only the cloud bot's wiring changes.

What is proven where (honest):
  OFFLINE (this PR, red->green):
    - C2 test_recordings.py: N counting-pattern chunks + empty is_final ->
      /recordings -> /master -> /raw byte-equals the build_recording_master oracle
      AND the arithmetic PCM oracle (A2/#491); a crashed 3-of-5 no-final recording
      stays in_progress yet /raw serves exactly the 3 parts (A1/#412); the empty-
      final fold never points storage at the signal chunk (A3 unit); a single
      is_final chunk still lists/masters/downloads (A4). The #491 direct-/raw case
      and the A3 unit go RED on reverting the jsonb/router hunks.
    - C1 recording.test.ts: each timeslice uploads immediately (seq-ordered) before
      any close; a mid-meeting kill leaves N parts durable (no all-or-nothing); the
      empty is_final is forwarded; close() synthesizes the final at most once; and
      over the real RecordingService HTTP wire, session_uid == inv.connectionId on
      every chunk. The P22/#224-class regression pin the 0.12 in-memory bot lacked.
  LIVE-ONLY (not in this PR):
    - C1's full page->Node->HTTP loss path is proven only by a live Lite-compose run
      (VEXA_RECORDING_TIMESLICE_MS small, >=2 parts, docker kill mid-meeting, then
      retrieve + play). The offline arm proves the sink half only.

Deferred (noted, not implemented here): C3 compose gate multi-chunk probe
(deploy/compose/tests/stack_test.py — live/docker); the docs.vexa.ai mdx pages;

seal the DB schema: gate:db-schema freezes tables+columns (no unreviewed DB changes) (#612)

The DB schema had no seal — a stray migration or model edit could add/drop/change
a table or column and land silently (there was no CI check that the schema is what

.seal.json freeze those surfaces.

- scripts/schema_digest.py — stdlib-ast digest of the SQLAlchemy schema-of-record
  (admin-api schema/models.py, which owns the tables) + meeting-api's mirror
  (sessions/models.py): {file: {table: {column: normalized Column(...) source}}}.
  No SQLAlchemy import, no DB — runs anywhere. Sorted, so only a real structural
  change moves the bytes (comments/formatting/column-reorder do not).
- schema.seal.json — the frozen digest: 68 columns across 9 tables (6 authoritative
  + 3 mirror). Human-readable + diffable; the diff IS the review surface.
- gate:db-schema (scripts/gates.mjs) recomputes the digest and fails on any ADDED /
  REMOVED / CHANGED column vs the seal, naming each. A deliberate change requires
  `pnpm seal:schema` (the seal-schema command) — a human lane:schema step.
- Wired into CI (package.json + gates.yml) beside gate:config-contract.

Proven: green at head; RED when a column is added (exact ADDED line); green when
reverted; seal:schema is idempotent. This is the structural enforcement of the
"no database changes without explicit sign-off" rule.

fix(meeting-api): reclaim a crashed replica's orphaned segment batch (#636) (#646)

* fix(meeting-api): reclaim a crashed replica's orphaned segment batch (#636)

Every meeting-api replica joined the collector consumer group under one
hard-coded name (`collector-main`) and there was no XAUTOCLAIM anywhere, so a
replica that crashed after XREADGROUP delivered a batch but before XACK left
those segments un-acked in its PEL forever — no surviving replica could
distinguish, let alone reclaim, them. The orphaned pending entry also pinned
the retention trim floor (db_writer), converting silent loss into silent
unbounded stream growth, and `/health` reported only undelivered lag so the
stall was invisible. Live under the stock `replicaCount: 2` helm default.

C1 — pod-identity consumer name + orphan reclaim (collector seam):
  * `CONSUMER_NAME` is now `COLLECTOR_CONSUMER_NAME` or `collector-<hostname>`
    (in k8s the pod name is the hostname) — distinct per replica.
  * new `RedisBus.reclaim_orphans` port (XAUTOCLAIM, min-idle gated),
    implemented in `RedisStreamBus` and mirrored in `FakeRedisBus`.
  * new `ingest.reclaim_segments` drains reclaimed entries through the SAME
    ingest -> ack path; folded into `_segment_consumer_loop` every N ticks,
    bounded to one XAUTOCLAIM per pass (cursor continues next tick — no hang
    surface). `COLLECTOR_RECLAIM_MIN_IDLE_MS` (default 60s) keeps a live peer's
    in-flight batch from being stolen.

C2 — PEL depth on `/health` (pipeline-health seam):
  * `_pipeline_health` adds a bounded (2s wait_for) group XPENDING summary ->
    `pipeline.pending_depth`; a total above `PIPELINE_PENDING_ALARM` (default
    100) flips status->degraded + 503, exactly like the lag alarm. A probe
    failure degrades the field to "unavailable", never blocks.

fix(terminal): cap and prune login-minted API tokens (#638) (#643)

findOrCreateUserToken minted a fresh bot,tx,browser API token on EVERY
OAuth/email sign-in with no lookup or teardown, so each login left one live,
never-expiring token forever — an OAuth redirect loop could flood a user's
account (hosted precedent: 1,888 phantom tokens across 101 users in ~3 days).

Since a minted secret is irretrievable after creation, reuse-the-secret is
impossible (list returns metadata only). The realizable bound is cap+prune:

- Mint login tokens via mintUserToken with a stable name "terminal-login" so
  they are distinguishable from user-created self-serve tokens.
- After minting, list the user's tokens, keep only name==="terminal-login",
  sort oldest-first, and revoke everything beyond the newest N
  (VEXA_TERMINAL_LOGIN_TOKEN_CAP, default 3).
- Never touch tokens with a different name (self-serve keys are left intact).
- Pruning is best-effort: list/revoke failures (e.g. a 404 on a concurrently
  deleted token) are logged and swallowed and never fail the sign-in.

Client-only change inside clients/terminal — no admin-api, contract, or schema
change (listUserTokens/mintUserToken/revokeToken already exist).

Adds vitest at findOrCreateUserToken.test.ts (fake admin-api recording
mint/list/revoke) covering A1 (K=6 sign-ins bound to 3, 3 oldest pruned),
A2 (self-serve + login mix: mint once, 0 revokes, self-serve untouched),
over-cap self-serve guard, a 404-mid-prune edge, and a fresh-user case.

Docs: clients/terminal/README.md and docs/docs/authentication.mdx describe the
terminal-login cap and that self-serve tokens are never pruned by login.

fix(meeting-api): single-flight background sweeps across replicas (#637) (#645)

* fix(meeting-api): single-flight background sweeps across replicas (#637)

At meetingApi.replicaCount>1 every meeting-api replica's FastAPI lifespan
started the same background loops with no leader election, so each sweep's
real work ran once per replica instead of once per interval — most sharply
calendar-sync, whose external ICS/Google fetch has no other dedup and so
doubled outbound requests to third-party calendar providers every interval.

V1 — Single-flight sweeps (structural): wrap each live tick body in a
per-loop Postgres session-level advisory lock (new meeting_api/sweeps/
single_flight.py). The two-arg pg_try_advisory_lock(SWEEP_LOCK_CLASSID,
crc32(loop_name)) form keeps the sweep keyspace disjoint from the single-arg
per-user pg_advisory_xact_lock(:user_id) locks. The load-bearing wrap is
calendar-sync; db-writer, webhook-drain, stop-reconcile and auto-join are
wrapped too. segment-consumer is DELIBERATELY left unguarded — it is a Redis
competing consumer whose single-delivery is already exact, and guarding it
would needlessly serialize the replicas' stream reads. With no DB session
factory (Lite single-replica, or a store without PG) the guard degrades to
run-the-tick, so single-replica behavior is unchanged.

V2 — Remove dead loop: the scheduler-tick task and its _scheduler_tick_loop
def are deleted from the same lifespan seam. app.state.scheduler was never
wired, so the loop returned immediately on every replica; the Scheduler in
scheduling/ is an eval-only engine and is left untouched.

Tests: tests/test_single_flight.py (FakeAdvisoryLock, two concurrent guarded
coroutines — the loser's body does not run; later uncontended tick does;
None-lock degrades; disjoint keyspace) and a test_app.py boot-set assertion
that the started loop names no longer contain scheduler-tick. Full suite
green (667 passed, 2 pre-existing skips).

fix(lite): an empty env flag must not silently disable transcription (#650) + unbreak `make up` (#651) (#652)

The v0.12.5 release witness: a bot joined a real Google Meet, was admitted, behaved
normally, and transcribed nothing — with no error anywhere. Both defects below are in

fix(meeting-api): reclaim degrades on Redis<6.2 (#636) + advisory-lock signature (#637) — v0.12.5 witness regressions (#649)

* fix(meeting-api): reclaim degrades on Redis<6.2 (#636) + advisory-lock signature (#637)

The v0.12.5 release witness caught two real regressions from the reliability batch — both
green in CI (fakes outran production), both crash-looping on real infrastructure:

#636 — reclaim_orphans called XAUTOCLAIM unconditionally; it needs Redis >= 6.2, but the Lite
image bundles Redis 6.0.16, so every segment-consumer tick raised `unknown command XAUTOCLAIM`
and the consumer died -> no transcription. Now it degrades to a no-op (logged once) when
XAUTOCLAIM is unsupported; the normal XREADGROUP consume path is unaffected. Unrelated
ResponseErrors still propagate.

#637 — the sweep guard used the two-arg pg_try_advisory_lock(classid, objid); crc32(objid)
overflows signed int4 -> asyncpg binds it as bigint -> pg_try_advisory_lock(int4, bigint), a
signature Postgres lacks -> every sweep (auto-join, calendar-sync, ...) crashed each tick. Now
a single 64-bit key ((SWEEP_LOCK_CLASSID<<32)|crc32) via the single-arg
pg_try_advisory_lock(bigint) form.

Root gap: the unit tests used fakes more capable than the shipped backends (fakeredis has
XAUTOCLAIM; FakeAdvisoryLock never runs the SQL). Added guards that catch this class below the
human witness: reclaim-degrades + over-swallow-control tests, a sweep-key int8-range test, a

gone (0 XAUTOCLAIM / advisory-lock errors after patching).

fix(release): the witness batch is bounded by the last release that SHIPPED, not the last tag (#658)

A tag is not a release. A candidate can be tagged, published, fail its witness, and be
abandoned — v0.12.5 was exactly that. prevTag() only asked whether a tag EXISTS, so an
abandoned candidate silently became the next release's baseline and its whole batch fell
through a hole: the last shipped release's receipt ends before those PRs, the next one's
begins after them, and no gate requires releases/<prevTag>/witness.json to exist.

Concretely, before this change: :v012 points at 0.12.4, so promoting v0.12.6 hands users
15 PRs — and the generated manifest listed 2, because prevTag(v0.12.6) resolved to the
abandoned v0.12.5. #626 (LOCAL_STT), #636, #637, #584, #633, #638 and the rest would have
reached users with no entry in any manifest. That is guarantee 7 failing exactly the way
the v0.12.1 incident failed it: promoted on machinery, witnessed by nobody.

The fix uses what already exists: releases/README.md says "the receipt is the record", so
the baseline is the greatest lower tag that HAS releases/<tag>/witness.json. An abandoned
candidate has no receipt and can never become a baseline — the hole closes structurally
rather than by convention, and no separate bookkeeping of "what shipped" is needed.

The rule: the batch is what the promote hands users — (last shipped) → (this version).

  after  → generated_from v0.12.4...v0.12.6, 15 entries, 4 user-visible / 11 by-proxy
and it logs the baseline it chose plus every candidate it skipped, so the decision is
visible rather than inferred.

fix(runtime): process backend reaps the whole process group on teardown (#546) (#661)

Every workload is spawned as its own process-group leader
(start_new_session=True), but nothing ever signalled the group — a
self-exiting or stopped bot orphaned every child it spawned (Chromium/node
tree) onto the shared Lite host, reparented to PID 1 and invisible to the
runtime's accounting.

Group-scoped teardown at the one seam (process_backend.py):
- _signal_group(pgid, sig): os.killpg on the leader pid==pgid;
  ProcessLookupError = group already gone (silent success), PermissionError
  degrades loudly (non-root runtime) and never crashes the caller.
- exit_code(): first observation of ANY exit (clean or not) sweeps the group
  once (one-shot guard) — covers the self-exit path (V1) and, via kernel.stop's
  polling, the graceful-stop path.
- kill()/cleanup(): SIGKILL the whole group (grace-expiry escalation).
- terminate(): stays leader-only SIGTERM (fork B1) — preserves the bot's
  graceful-leave contract; the group sweep rides the observed exit + kill().

docker/k8s backends and kernel.py untouched (container semantics already tear
down the tree). Tests: A1 self-exit orphan fixture, A2 stop-path fixture (both
RED on base, GREEN after), plus the childless-workload silent-reap edge. Docs:
runtime.mdx, README, troubleshooting note the whole-tree guarantee and the
detached-grandchildren limitation.

fix(merge-card): treat non-terminal value-fsm as pending, wait for a verdict (#655) (#665)

`labeled` fires merge-card AND re-triggers value-fsm, so the newest value-fsm
run on head is frequently still queued/in_progress (conclusion === null) when the
card evaluates. valueFsmVerdict collapsed that non-terminal run into "failure",
red-carding a PR whose value-fsm was on its way to green — every value-signed PR
needed a manual `gh run rerun`.

- verdictFromRuns() is now four-state: absent | pending | success | failure
  (queued|in_progress ⇒ pending, not failure). Pure + exported for unit tests.
- waitForTerminalValueFsm() polls the head sha until value-fsm reaches a terminal
  read (success|failure) within a bounded budget, removing the race. A run that
  never settles stays pending/absent and the card red-cards it LOUDLY — success
  must be positively observed; a label can never waive value-fsm.
- card() consumes the waited verdict; distinct pending/absent vs terminal-failure
  card copy so the audit trail no longer asserts "is failure" about a running check.
- module main guarded behind import.meta.url so tests can import the seams.
- ADR-0030 + header comment: non-terminal value-fsm yields pending, not failure.

Closes #660.

degrades to a logged no-op on a Redis without XINFO CONSUMERS, exactly as
reclaim_orphans does for XAUTOCLAIM (Lite bundles Redis 6.0.16).

  reclaim_segments after the orphan reclaim.

- tests: A1 (ghost pruned past TTL, via sweep), A2 (pending>0 never pruned

fix(#520): crash-safe Redis reliable-queue for the webhook retry drain (#614)

* fix(#520): crash-safe Redis reliable-queue for the webhook retry drain

Root cause (loss mode #3, verified at head). The webhook retry drain
(`webhooks/retry.py:drain_retry_queue`) LPOPped every queued entry into a
process-local `requeue` list and RPUSHed the not-yet-due / rescheduled ones back
to Redis only at the END of the sweep. A worker crash — or Redis failing —
between the LPOP and that final RPUSH lost every entry popped in that sweep: the
recovery mechanism itself dropped envelopes (the one most likely to matter,
`meeting.completed`, is the only default-enabled event).

Fix. Rewrite the drain as the classic Redis reliable-queue pattern, entirely in
Redis (no schema, no DB, no new dependency):
  * each entry is atomically claimed with RPOPLPUSH from `webhook:retry_queue`
    into a processing list `webhook:retry_processing` — it is NEVER held only in
    process memory;
  * it is then resolved individually — ack → LREM from processing; reschedule →
    re-queue (bumped attempt + next backoff) then LREM; exhausted / aged-out →
    dead-letter then LREM; not-yet-due → returned to the queue then LREM. Re-queue
    is push-before-LREM, so a crash duplicates rather than loses;
  * a crash leaves the in-flight entry in the processing list; every tick first

fix(db-budget-gate): the pool scan counts production source — make the test filter express it (#702) (#704)

_explicitPool() ended `… | grep -v test`, downstream of a `-h` scan. `-h` (with -o)
strips the filename, so the pipeline emitted bare matches (`pool_size=6`) and the
filter was matching "test" against text that carries no path. It removed nothing —
every pool literal under core/**/*.py entered a budget whose unit is
Σ(helm replicas × pool ceiling), tests included.

DECISION: tests are excluded. A test's engine is a throwaway no deployment runs. It
holds zero production connections, so a pool literal in a test cannot under-state the
budget — counting one could only invent a red against a service whose deployed pool is
whatever its production source says. This is the contract gateDbBudget() already states
in its own error text ("no non-test source constructs a DB engine there") and the
population _dbHoldingServices() already reads; both now share one _isTestPath, so the
two scans cannot drift apart on what "a service's code" means.

- `-no`, never `-h`: the path has to survive the scan to be filtered on. The parse is
  anchored to git grep's whole `path:lineno:match` record (-o makes the match the entire
  final field), so a path spelling "pool_size=99" can never be read as the literal — the
  old first-match regex reads 99 out of such a path and reds. -o is kept because it
  splits two literals on one source line into two records; without it the second hides.
- The path test is basename-precise, and both directions have counterexamples in this
  tree: `includes("test_")` drops production files (latest_pool.py) out of a PRODUCTION
  budget — the one direction this gate must never fail — while pytest's other convention,
  the *_test.py suffix, names production source here (core/agent/control_plane/
  config_test.py implements the Settings → Models "Test" buttons). Reclassifies 0 of 348
  tracked core/**/*.py files; it closes a hole rather than moving the line.
- The under-count error now names the file:line it read the literal from. The scan is
  repo-wide ("a match anywhere raises the floor"), so it reports a number against a
  service that may set nothing — a bare number with no file is what sent #702's report,
  and its first draft, chasing SQLAlchemy for what was a numpy fixture.

feat(bot): fail-fast control-plane reachability gate before join (Refs #530) (#781)

The C2 half of #530: a bot that cannot reach its control plane now refuses to
join and terminates with a typed, attributed outcome instead of an opaque
crashloop or a generic join_failure.

Mechanism (orchestrator seam, one module):
- The FIRST `joining` lifecycle emit is load-bearing. The HTTP sink gains
  `emitReachable` (ports.PrimaryReachability): any HTTP response = reachable
  (P18 — the channel is up); only an all-attempts network failure (the
  fresh-node CNI-lag signature) is `unreachable`. Reachable ⇒ zero added
  latency (the secondary channel is never probed).
- On primary-unreachable, the orchestrator probes the secondary channel
  (redis PING, injected ControlPlaneProbe). Either channel up ⇒ proceed;
  BOTH down ⇒ refuse to join before any meeting navigation.
- The refusal terminates `failed` / `failure_stage: requested` with a dedicated
  exit code 3 (the attributable signal on k8s bare Pods) and the machine-readable
  attribution `infra_fault: control_plane_unreachable` + `unreachable_channels`.
- Reachability retry budget is bounded (≤ ~15s) — rides out transient CNI
  programming, far under the meeting-api `requested` grace.

No contract change (C2 fork-4): the sealed lifecycle.v1 CompletionReason enum
is untouched — attribution rides an existing reason (`join_failure`) +
`failure_stage: requested` + the additive `infra_fault` field (LifecycleEvent
additionalProperties:true) + exit 3. gate:contract-version stays green.

Tests (offline, red→green): L2 orchestrator — both-down ⇒ no join, exit 3,
control_plane_unreachable; either-channel-up ⇒ proceed; primary-reachable ⇒
proceed with the secondary never probed. L3 lifecycle-http — emitReachable
reachable/503-reachable/all-network-error-unreachable/transient fixtures.

Docs: bot README (pre-join gate seam + exit-code table), deployment-kubernetes
(autoscaling and bot bursts), troubleshooting (exit code 3), changelog fragment.

The attribution half (C1 probe / V1) stays open — it needs cluster evidence.

fix(meeting-api): shared-meetings list — UNION-split access branches + per-branch indexes (#800) (#801)

* fix(meeting-api): shared-meetings list — UNION-split access branches + per-branch indexes; OR-plan scanned the whole created_at index (#800)

The list_meetings access predicate (owner OR transcript-share viewer OR
workspace member) planned as Index Scan Backward over created_at with the
OR as a Filter: worst-case callers scanned ~the whole table per call
(measured 220ms/400k-row scan at bench scale; 100s+ on prod, where the
resulting pool saturation rolled back the hosted 0.12.12 cutover).

Each access branch is now its own top-N indexed subquery merged by
UNION ALL, deduped and re-ordered by the outer query. Supporting indexes
(both schema mirrors): (user_id, created_at) btree, jsonb_path_ops GIN on
(data->'transcript_viewers'), ((data->>'workspace_id'), created_at) btree.

Measured (PG16, 400k rows, worst-case caller: 3 old owned + 2 shared):
old 220.8ms / 402k buffers / 399,998 rows filtered → new 0.104ms / 33
buffers; result sets identical (ordered id arrays equal). Live-adapter
checks: ordering, pagination slice, workspace branch, non-list path,
heavy-user has_more — all green. Deployers build the three indexes
CONCURRENTLY before rolling the image (in-band CREATE INDEX locks
meetings under live traffic).

plan (the JSONB containment branch loses the GIN path without the
parameter value and falls back to the backward created_at walk).

fix(meeting-api): report every webhook delivery outcome — non-delivery was silent (#815) (#817)

WebhookSink.deliver returns delivered|suppressed|blocked|failed|queued
and never raises; app.py discarded the result. A webhook the subscriber

successful delivery logged nothing, so 'my webhooks stopped' could not

fix(config): a wrong STT URL or token is caught where you set it, not by an empty transcript (#511) (#823)

Three consumers green-lit configurations that cannot transcribe, so the first
evidence of a bad backend was an empty transcript mid-meeting.

C1 — the probe's oracle. `_http_probe` treated ANY status but 401/403 as proof of
a working endpoint, so the most common misconfiguration (a URL whose
transcriptions path 404s) probed green. A declaration-driven `invalid_statuses`
([404] for stt) now demotes it to `misconfigured` with a reason. 400 stays
proof-of-life: a real OpenAI-compatible endpoint answers 400/401 to an empty
body and never 404.

C2 — the wizard's green. On any non-Vexa endpoint the test probed `/balance`,
got 404, and returned PASS with "token was not verified". A rejected key tested
green and failed mid-meeting. It now falls through to the same request a bot's
first audio chunk makes and grades the endpoint's own answer.

C3 — the spawn gate. POST /bots refuses a set-but-misconfigured backend with a
typed 503 carrying the probe's reason, before the meeting row is written. Three
bounds keep the refusal honest: cached verdicts only (no probe I/O on the
request path), CONFIG faults only (`unauthorized`/`invalid_endpoint` — refusing
on `unreachable` would fail every spawn for a minute whenever STT restarts), and
the env backend only (a Settings-configured backend is a different endpoint).

C4 — one URL contract. A full `…/v1/audio/transcriptions` URL worked in meetings
but double-pathed into a 404 in the probe and the dictation route. All four
consumers now share the client's rule: append only when absent.

config.v1 gains one optional property (`invalid_statuses`, default []) and
probe failures gain `kind`, so a consumer can tell "fix your config" from "the
endpoint is down". Back-compatible; the seal moves for config.v1 only.

Closes #511

fix(lifecycle): a bot that was never admitted is not a completed meeting (#807) (#824)

Stopping a bot still sitting in the waiting room wrote `stopping` over its real
status, destroying the only record of the stage it died in. Every downstream
reader then concluded the bot had been live: `reconcile._WAS_ACTIVE_STATUSES`
completes a `stopping` row, and `machine._PERSISTED_STATUS_TO_BOTSTATUS`
rehydrates it as ACTIVE. So a run that never joined and produced no transcript
was persisted as `completed` — the system reporting success for a total value
failure — over an `awaiting_admission → completed` edge LEGAL_TRANSITIONS does
not contain, waved through by `force_terminal_on_destroy`.

Current-era repro, on the deployed build (meeting-api 0.12.14-260719-hc12,
2026-07-19): meeting 24336's own transition log records the illegal edge —
joining → awaiting_admission (bot_callback, 12:19:14Z), then
awaiting_admission → completed (runtime_destroy, 12:20:01Z, "stopped"),
zero transcript segments. The deployed image contains the defect line
(stop_router.py:107, read from the running pod). Era note: the "49% of
zero-segment completions" figure that motivated #807 was measured over
prior-era (hosted-compat) rows; the current-era share is TBD once post-cutover
data accumulates. The mechanism, not the share, is what this fixes.

Fixed at the producer. `stopping` now means what the rest of the chain already
assumed it meant: a LIVE bot is being asked to leave. A stop against a
pre-active bot leaves the stage in place, so the terminal classifier reads real
evidence instead of a side-effect, and such a run ends `failed` with
`failure_stage` naming where it actually died. The two comments that asserted
the false premise now state the invariant the fix guarantees.

Retry class follows. A user stop before admission earns `stopped` — the sealed
user-terminal reason, PERMANENT — not `awaiting_admission_timeout`, which is
TRANSIENT and would re-spawn a bot three times against a meeting the user
deliberately walked away from, on their own quota. An admission wait that times
out on its own is untouched and still retried.

reading a status side-effect, and only held against the in-memory test double —
the SQL adapter's active set contains `stopping`, so in production a redelivered
DELETE found the row and published a second leave command. The guard is now the
recorded user intent, which is true at every stage.

fix(join): Zoom/Teams admission verdicts are typed — permanent failures stop being retried (#806) (#827)

The AdmissionOutcome contract (shared/admission.ts) existed and the driver
mapping (join-driver.ts) was already correct — but only Google Meet and Jitsi
threw it. Every Zoom and Teams admission failure was a bare Error, so
`instanceof AdmissionError` missed it, the orchestrator blanket-mapped it to
transient `join_failure`, and retry.py re-spawned bots against verdicts no
retry can change: a Zoom host denial re-knocked 3×, the RTMS anti-bot wall was
retried into the same wall, an auth-restricted meeting was rejoined signed-out.

Typed now, at every terminal site:
  * zoom/admission.ts — host rejection → denial; RTMS wall → denial (a
    distinct `blocked` CompletionReason needs lane:contract, noted in the
    driver); poll timeout → lobby_timeout.
  * zoom/join.ts — the signed-in-users-only wall → auth_session_missing (the
    same sealed outcome the dead-profile path uses; already PERMANENT).
  * msteams/admission.ts — denial → denial (the message was byte-identical to
    the Google Meet path that typed it); both lobby-timeout throws →
    lobby_timeout.
  * googlemeet/admission.ts — the one straggler plain-Error lobby conclusion →
    lobby_timeout.

Teams had a second layer: an outer catch re-wrapped EVERY throw into a plain
Error, so even a typed verdict would have been flattened. It now re-throws
AdmissionError unchanged (the googlemeet idiom). Genuinely indeterminate
failures stay plain Errors — no over-typing; transient join_failure remains
their honest class.

Tests drive the SHIPPED waits over fabricated pages (the jitsi pattern):
zoom/admission.test.ts and msteams/admission.test.ts, each case shaped to
conclude before the escalation module's 5-minute extension can latch.

Beyond correctness this makes the modes measurable: they land in
completion_reason per platform, which is the first half of the #806 taxonomy.
The structured join_failure_code field remains open on the issue.

fix(meeting-api): answer /bots/status from the query, not from the whole account (#803) (#825)

A running-bots badge read every meeting the caller ever had, with the full
`data` JSONB, and filtered in Python. On a production account that is 4,896
meetings / 180 MB — 144 MB of it `bot_logs`, which no endpoint renders. Four
concurrent polls landed on one pod within 400 ms and demanded roughly 740 MB
transiently; the pod OOM-killed at the default 1 GiB limit.

This is peak memory, not a retention leak: three identical pods sat at wildly
different plateaus (712 vs 1342 MiB) and RSS stepped rather than sloped, which
is what per-request high-water marks look like and what a leak does not.

The #584 outage fix introduced exactly the right mechanism — a status/heavy-key
projection — but exempted the "internal enumeration" callers. `/bots/status` is
not internal enumeration; it is a user-facing polling endpoint. That exemption
is the defect, so the fix is at the query:

  * `status` accepts a SET, so the five non-terminal statuses are selected in
    SQL instead of scanned in Python;
  * `slim` applies the existing heavy-key projection to a non-list caller that
    renders none of those keys either.

Both halves are load-bearing. The filter bounds the rows, the projection bounds
each row, and stuck non-terminal rows (98 in production) mean the filter alone
is not a cap.

`GET /meetings/{id}` had the same shape at smaller scale — it enumerated the
account to find one row. It now constrains by id in SQL, under the same access
union, and still returns full `data`: the detail view is exactly where every key
belongs.

* bot: idempotent memoized redis connect (fix "Socket already opened" race)

The transcript writer and acts subscriber connect lazily on first use, memoizing
with a boolean flipped only AFTER connect() resolves. That is a check-then-act race:
the first `await client.connect()` yields the loop before the flag is set, so a second
concurrent first-use caller also sees it false and calls connect() again — node-redis
v4 throws "Socket already opened" on the second (observed as a bot pipeline fault).

Extract the connect memo into a shared makeLazyConnect() that memoizes the connect
PROMISE (concurrent callers share one connect); a failed connect clears the memo so a
later call retries; quit() settles any in-flight connect and only quit()s an open socket.
Both adapters now use it, removing the duplicated fragile pattern.

Adds redis-lazy-connect.test.ts: a negative control proves the old flag-after-await memo
double-connects (red); makeLazyConnect connects once under the same concurrency (green),
plus retry-after-failure and quit-settles-in-flight.

* fix(bot): bound quit()'s wait for an in-flight redis connect

Regression introduced by the #822 memo and confirmed by an adversarial batch review, then
reproduced independently: quit() awaited the memoized connect unconditionally. node-redis v4's
DEFAULT reconnectStrategy retries forever, so connect() against an unreachable server stays
PENDING — it neither resolves nor rejects — and teardown hung. The pre-#822 boolean memo
returned immediately in that case, so this was a real regression on the exit path: a bot whose
redis is down would never exit.

The settle-first intent is kept (quit must not race a half-open socket); the wait is now bounded
by quitSettleMs (default 5s) with an unref'd timer, after which teardown proceeds on isOpen.

* fix(bot): a delivered frame is presence — drop the redundant RMS floor on aloneness

Capture is the single silence oracle. The page emits a frame only when its PEAK sample clears
the capture gate (mixed-audio.ts:54 / gmeet-capture.ts:41, 0.005), and the activity tap sits on
the Node side of that gate (capture-bridge.ts:289,298). Every frame reaching the tap has already
proven it carries audio — and was sent to STT and transcribed on that basis.

The tap then re-judged the same frame by RMS against the SAME 0.005. RMS is always <= peak (for
speech 3-5x lower), so that second test could only REJECT audio capture had accepted, never admit
anything it refused: a pure false-negative generator. A participant speaking quietly was
transcribed while counting as silence toward left_alone — the bot could leave a meeting it could
hear. #850 measured 23.3% of frames in a real fixture sitting in exactly that band.

A cost decision (don't pay Whisper for near-silence) is not a presence decision. Floor is now 0;
only a zero/non-finite reading is silence.

Renegotiates the prior assertion 'near-silent remote frames do not reset', which encoded the
false-negative as intent. Replaced by two guards: a quiet delivered frame is presence, and a
zero-energy frame is not. Floor restored -> the quiet guard goes red; zero guard unaffected.

Contribution policy: a corporate contributor can start the process themselves (#1095)

* Contribution policy: a corporate contributor can start the process themselves

Publish CLA/employer-authorization-template.md. The corporate path required
Vexa to email a rights holder's counsel and ask them to compose a confirmation
meeting seven criteria. Drafting is the slow step in legal review, and it put
Vexa in cold contact with another company's legal department just to begin.
Inverted: the contributor forwards a short letter to their own open-source
approvers, who fill in their details and sign. It grants Vexa nothing --
Apache-2.0 Section 5 already places contributions under the project license
unless the submitter states otherwise, so the letter confirms only that the
submitter is authorized, and adds no Vexa terms to negotiate. One letter covers
past, present and future contributions, so nobody repeats this per pull request.

No limitations field and no ownership or third-party-material warranty: an
organization's internal constraints are theirs to manage with their employee,
not conditions Vexa reasons about per pull request. A fallback clause grants on
Apache-2.0 terms and no others where Section 5 does not reach the organization
directly, and withdrawal is stated as prospective only, since licenses already
granted under Sections 2 and 3 are irrevocable by their own terms.

Remove five stale promises of a licensed-counsel approval step Vexa is not
going to run: 2 in CLA/README.md, 2 in CONTRIBUTOR_RIGHTS.md, 1 in
docs/adr/0034-contributor-rights-gate.md, whose status is proposed and is
therefore amended rather than superseded. grep -rn counsel returns zero hits.

Vexa now publishes no contributor agreement at all, and asks no one to sign
one. Publishing an unadopted draft while insisting it was not an offer was the
awkward part of the previous shape; not publishing one removes the risk, the
hash-pinning ceremony, and the question of what is operative. One route is
maintained, not a menu -- every published route goes stale, contradicts its
siblings, and must be re-verified whenever anything around it moves, so a
second earns its place only by carrying value the first cannot. A legal team
that requires a signed instrument regardless is told to email us, and one gets
built when a real counterparty needs it.

Add an agent runbook for DCO sign-off so the human never handles Git ceremony.
Git has no commit.signoff setting -- format.signOff affects format-patch only,
and Git's own docs note the trailer should be a conscious act, which the
human's rights-path choice satisfies. The runbook installs a repository-local
prepare-commit-msg hook that uses the contributor's own configured identity, is
idempotent against -s, and exits quietly on unset identity; it includes a
verification step, because a silent hook failure looks exactly like success.
Verified working before publication. The line an agent does not cross is
restated: install and verify the mechanism, never choose the rights path, never
sign for anyone else.

Receipt format, private register, head-SHA binding and DCO requirements are
unchanged.
