fix(teams): account for every tile, and name which indicator fired

Measured on v0.12.18 in a live 13-minute Teams meeting (4-6 participants, two
people conversing): SPEAKER_START 0, SPEAKER_END 2 (bootstrap silent assertions
only), "Scanned 4 participants, observing 1 with signal" x127 then "Scanned 6,
observing 2" x22 — the counts never moved — and all 37 transcript rows labelled
"Speaker". The same build named speakers correctly on Google Meet.

Two gates were failing, both silently.

Gate A — a tile without `[data-tid="voice-level-stream-outline"]` was skipped
with a bare `return`, so 3 of 4 participants were INVISIBLE: not observed, not
named, and not reported as missing. The rule is unchanged (no signal, no hint —
ever), but every matched tile is now counted and an outline-less one emits a
typed `signal-absent` observation carrying no DOM text, no display name and no
tile id. The scan line reports the absent count; a coverage ratio below 0.5
logs one WARN.

Gate B — speaking was a single hardcoded `vdi-frame-occlusion` class test, which
never fired once in 13 minutes. It is a VDI frame-occlusion marker, not a speech
indicator, and the stability of the tile counts shows outline PRESENCE is
structural per-tile, not speech-tracking. Guessing its replacement is how we got
here, so speaking is now an ORDERED list of named candidate predicates evaluated
on the outline and its ancestors — vdi-occlusion (kept verbatim, it fired at
least once historically), inline-style-motion (the observer already watched
`style` and the detector only ever tested `class`), aria-state, class-token-delta
(records WHICH token) — the first to fire wins, and an `indicator-fired`
observation names it. A live run now reports the truth instead of us theorising.

inline-style-motion requires the tile to have shown >=3 distinct style
signatures before a change counts as speech: a voice bar rewrites its geometry
many times a second, a layout reflow rewrites it once and holds. Without that
floor one resize makes every tile read as speaking, which attributes speech to
the WRONG person — worse than silence.

Fail loud — `indicator-silent` fires (and WARNs) when tiles are observable and
nothing has entered the speaking state for a window (default 60s), and health()
exposes {found, observable, named, nameUnresolved, transitions}. These are
diagnostics: none of them can become a speaker hint. The hysteresis, debounce,
self-name filter and no-blank-name guard are unchanged, and nothing here invents
a name — unknown stays unknown.

Tests: teams-speaker-indicators.test.ts — offline DOM shim, hand-driven rAF and
an injected clock (the 60s window is exercised without sleeping). Includes a
regression that pins the production failure exactly: 4 tiles, 1 outline, no
indicator ever fires => 0 hints, 3 signal-absent, coverage-low WARN, and
indicator-silent.

fix(teams): hold edge indicators as levels — the hint path was dead

An end-to-end rehearsal in real headless Chromium showed the detector working
and onSpeaking never being called: transitions=3, indicator-fired x3, HINTS [],
and no SPEAKER_START log line at all. Diagnostics alive, hint path dead — Teams
still produced zero attribution. Reproduced locally before changing anything,
and again in headless Chromium after.

ROOT CAUSE. Candidates come in two shapes and I conflated them. vdi-occlusion
and aria-state are LEVELS: they answer "is this tile speaking right now" on any
sample. inline-style-motion and class-token-delta are EDGES: they answer "did
something just change", which is true on exactly the one sample that observes
the change and false on every sample in between. Speaking is a level. With rAF
sampling at ~60fps and a voice bar updating every ~150ms, an edge read raw is
true on 1 sample in 9, so the level flapped at the sampling rate. The 200ms
hysteresis then admitted an alternating transition roughly every 200ms, and
because the 300ms debounce is LONGER than 200ms, each pending emit was cancelled
by the opposite transition before it could fire. Proved by construction: with
debounceMs=0 the same run yields 3 START/END pairs instead of none.

FIX. A candidate now declares kind: 'level' | 'edge'; an edge is held for
indicatorHoldMs (default 400ms, comfortably above the gap between two voice-bar
updates) and read as a level. A continuously animating outline is then speaking
on EVERY sample: one admitted transition, one START; when the animation stops
the hold expires and one END follows. Verified in headless Chromium over the
real bundle and the real bridge: transitions=1, one SPEAKER_START edge, one
SPEAKER_END edge.

On the coordinator's suspects, honestly: the debounce-reset suspect was right
and is the proximate mechanism. The hysteresis suspect was wrong in its details
— silent->speaking was not rejected, it was ADMITTED three times, which is why
indicator-fired fired three times. The >=3-signature floor was not the cause;
it gates only the first two changes and removing it fixes nothing. And
indicator-fired is emitted from the same code path that schedules the emit, two
statements apart, so that suspect was wrong too.

WHY THE UNIT TESTS MISSED IT, and what now stops that. Every shim block drove
exactly ONE sample per DOM change, so it never produced the between-updates
samples where the level collapsed. Two things close it:
  - teams-speaker-indicators.test.ts gains a REALISTIC CADENCE block that uses
    real timers, a real 16ms frame interval and the real 300ms debounce; with
    the hold reverted it reproduces the production symptom exactly (HINTS [],
    transitions=3, indicator-fired x3).
  - teams-speaker-animation.boundary.test.ts is new: the REAL bundle in real
    headless Chromium through the real startCaptureBridge, asserting one START
    edge and one END edge for an animating tile and zero hints for a tile with
    no outline. Green-or-skip where chromium is absent, same shape as
    capture-bridge.boundary.test.ts. With the hold reverted it goes red on
    transitions=3 and zero SPEAKER_START edges.

Note on hint cardinality: a turn longer than the 2s heartbeat yields extra START
HINTS, because the heartbeat deliberately re-asserts the current speaker for a
consumer that joined mid-turn (grafted from PR965, mirroring Zoom, idempotent at
the binder). Those are re-assertions, not edges — they carry the same name, sit
inside the turn, and emit no SPEAKER_START. The test asserts exactly that rather
than deleting the heartbeat.

Safety properties unchanged: no hint without signal, no blank or fabricated
name, self-name filtering, and a single reflow still does not read as speech
(the >=3-signature floor stays).

fix(teams): follow the evidence while a turn is open, lock the name at close

Attribution was sticky on the FIRST tick that produced any name at all
(chunked-transcriber.ts:706, `if (turn.resolvedName) return turn.resolvedName`).
The submit pump ticks about once a second, so that first tick decided a turn whose
commit window was still a fraction of a second: whoever's tile happened to be lit at
the onset owned the whole utterance. On Teams the tile lights on NOISE, so the other
participant TYPING at the moment a turn began stamped his name over all of it.

Measured on the first real Teams tape (meeting 24, 2 speakers, 569 hints). Over the
window the speakers themselves attest is Dmitry — 1786397358.0-1786397406.5, where he
describes the teams-capture module — the hints name Dmitry for 145.4s of lit time
against Jacob's 47.2s, better than 3:1, and the transcript said Jacob for all of it.
The evidence was there; the lock was taken before it arrived.

While a turn is OPEN, keep re-resolving over the grown window, and let a different
name take the turn only on a clear majority of the current window's support
(REATTRIBUTE_MIN_CONFIDENCE, 0.75, above the 0.6 first-attribution gate). Repaint
what the turn already published through the same rename path a late hint uses. At
close, lock: the window can grow no further.

This is strictly MORE evidence, never invented evidence. Two tiles lit for a whole
turn — genuinely ambiguous, and the platform-inherent half of the defect — still
resolves to nothing and still publishes as "Speaker".

Also lands the tape-replay harness this was measured with: it drives the REAL
ChunkedTranscriber from a captured-signal.v1 tape offline (injected segmenter, stub
STT, no model, no network), and it must run --realtime, because a defect that lives
in the submit cadence is invisible when the tape is fired instantly.

fix(teams): claim an unnamed turn by the hint record, not by who fired next

The dominant misattribution path on the first real Teams tape is not the window
match — it is the late-box claim at chunked-transcriber.ts:362. A turn that could
not be window-matched went to WHICHEVER NAME'S HINT HAPPENED TO FIRE NEXT, with no
requirement that the name was lit during the turn at all.

On Teams the voice-level outline reacts to NOISE, not speech — the speakers worked
this out during the meeting itself ("they react on noise"). A participant who is
TYPING therefore emits hints continuously and won that race nearly every time.
Meeting 24 labelled a balanced two-speaker conversation Jacob 65 : Dmitry 1, and
replaying the tape attributes 42 of those labels to this path. Naming a turn by who
happened to make a keystroke is fabrication: a confident name chosen by timing
rather than by evidence.

Read the accumulated lit-time over the turn's OWN window instead (ClusterNameBinder
now exposes `support()`, the aggregation windowMatch already computed), and claim
only when one name holds a clear plurality of it — CLAIM_MIN_SHARE, 0.6. The genuine
late-box gap, where no tile was lit during the turn at all and the platform reported
the speaker only afterwards, is unchanged and still claims for the firing hint;
claim.smoke pins that. What changes is only the contested case, which is exactly
where "whoever fired last" was choosing against the record.

Measured by replaying the m24 tape at 1x through the real transcriber:

                          before   after
  renames issued             42       3
  turns labelled Jacob       65      43
  labels over ground truth  5 right  3 right
                            1 wrong  0 wrong
                            6 unattributed  9 unattributed

That is the honest shape of this fix and it should not be oversold. It removes
fabricated confidence; it does not recover the right name. Both tiles are lit
simultaneously for 250s of this 425s meeting, and with one mixed audio stream and no
diarization in this lane there is no evidence left to break those ties — so those
turns now publish as "Speaker". Unknown stays unknown.

fix(transcript): promote a confirmed turn's dangling draft tail on close (never lose speech)

The pending-retract dedup made clearPending an actual delete, but the transcriber's
'never lose a turn' promotion only rescued a turn that confirmed NOTHING (seq===0). A

old drafts in one operation. Regression test never-lose-tail covers the seq>0 close path.

test(mixed): mirror the bot's pending retract into the tape-replay harness

The harness drives ChunkedTranscriber's callbacks directly, so it saw only the
UPSERT half of the durable store. The bot (services/bot/src/pipeline.ts) also diffs
the pending id set each pass and retracts the ids that dropped out, which the
collector turns into a DELETE. Without that leg the harness reports a durable store
the product does not have — it would have shown 42 draft leftovers that the shipped
stack removes.

test(mixed): emit the replayed rows as JSON, from the same run as the text

--out renders display text only, so loading a durable store from a replay meant a
second run — and STT output varies between runs, so the text file and the rows would
describe different transcripts. --out-json dumps the same post-retract durable map
the stats and the text render already read: segment_id, epoch start/end, speaker,
text. One run, one transcript, three consistent views of it.

fix(teams): transcribe only the mainAudio mix; dedup double-mirrored tracks

Teams delivers the entire meeting as ONE server-side audio mix (track id prefixed
"mainAudio") — witnessed live: the standard web client holds exactly one audio
receiver even while a specific person speaks. But Teams also hands the bot a second,
redundant track whose audio is already inside that mix. The mixed lane combined both,
so every word was fed to the transcriber twice → repeated words ("end the call" twice).

Teams now mixes ONLY the mainAudio track (the complete mix); Jitsi still combines all
tracks (its topology isn't witnessed). If no mainAudio track is present it waits rather
than combining two streams, and logs once.

Separately, the RTCPeerConnection hook mirrored each remote track twice — both
addEventListener('track') and the ontrack-setter wrapper fired handleTrack for the same
event. Deduped by track id so each track yields one <audio> element.

Signed-off-by: Jacob Schooley <jacob@schooley.com>
(cherry picked from commit 7853f8b78d8f00d8a21350e4e5357437706b63fe)

fix(teams): fail open when the mainAudio mix never appears, and keep saying so

Hardening on top of Jacob's mainAudio filter, which is right about the defect: Teams
delivers the whole meeting as one server-side mix, hands the bot a second redundant
track whose audio is already inside it, and combining both fed every word to the
transcriber twice.

The filter selects that mix by STRING MATCH on a vendor-generated track id, and
preferring it unconditionally introduces a worse failure than the one it fixes. When
Teams renames or drops the prefix — the same class of rot that already killed this
platform's class-based name selectors, on this platform, this month — the filter
matches nothing, `streams` is empty, `if (!streams.length) return` fires forever, and
the bot sits in the meeting recording SILENCE for its whole duration. It announces
that once, at minute zero, behind a latched `__vexaTeamsNoMainWarned`, and looks
healthy for the rest of the call. A doubled transcript is bad. An absent one is worse,
and it is the one nobody notices until the meeting is over.

So: prefer the mix whenever it exists; if none has appeared within a grace window
(15s, VEXA_TEAMS_MAIN_AUDIO_GRACE_MS), capture every track exactly as the pre-fix code
did and emit a typed `main-audio-absent` observation naming the condition and the
track ids actually seen — so a rotted prefix is diagnosable from the log alone. The
observation re-emits on EVERY falling-back rescan. No latch: a degraded capture that
reports itself once and then goes quiet is indistinguishable from a healthy one.

The decision lives in mixed-capture-core (`selectTeamsMixStreams`) rather than inside
the page callback, because the page callback is serialized into the browser and cannot
be unit-tested — a hand-copied twin next to it would drift from its test on the first
edit. The bundle already ships this module, so the page and the test run one
implementation.

Jacob's commit is untouched; this only adds the fallback path beneath it.

Tests: teams-main-audio.test.ts (12 checks — mix wins when present, silence inside
grace, fail-open past it, re-emits, recovers when the mix arrives late) and
webrtc-dedup.test.ts, which pins his double-mirror fix: one track event yields n=2
mirrored streams without the dedup and n=1 with it.

build(bot): ship selectTeamsMixStreams in the browser bundle

The page callback reaches it as w.VexaBrowserUtils.selectTeamsMixStreams; the bundle's
export list is explicit, so without this the call silently resolves to undefined and
setupMix falls back to capturing every stream — the pre-fix behaviour, with no
observation to say so.

fix(mixed): stop the segmenter's silence verdict from deleting speech

Only audio inside a turn is ever submitted, so a stretch pyannote calls silence is
not merely uncut — it is never transcribed. Measured on CLEAN audio with a Deepgram
oracle (new src/clean-audio-replay.ts, 270s single-speaker fixture): the streaming
segmenter declared 131.5s of 270s as speech and 79 of the oracle's 251 words fell
outside every declared region. Whisper straight through the same file scored 7.5%
WER against the oracle; the lane scored 27.2%, and the difference was almost entirely
words that were never sent.

The inter-turn gap now rides along with the next turn's window when it carries energy,
bounded (400ms..10s, VEXA_GAP_RECLAIM_MAX_MS) and skipped when the gap is genuinely
silent — Whisper hallucinates on silence, so that half matters as much as the other.
Only the STT window widens: t0, the window the namer resolves over, is untouched, so
speaker identification and retract behaviour are unchanged.

Scored on two clean fixtures, pipeline vs the same Whisper straight through:
  270s: 25.1% → 22.3% WER      165s: 23.9% → 15.9% WER
and against the Deepgram oracle: 27.2% → 24.0% and 30.3% → 23.1%.

Also lands VEXA_TRACE_SPANS — every window the lane submits and every one it declines.
Without it there is no way to tell "STT heard it and got it wrong" from "we never sent
that audio", which is the whole distinction this change rests on.

feat(identity): resolve capture_signal on bot-context — default ON, kill switch below it

Fixture collection needs prod meetings to tape by default, so the flag's absence
means ON: a deployment that has never heard of it still produces fixtures. What
the flag buys is the stop — PUT /internal/settings/diagnostics
{"capture_signal":"false"} and every subsequent spawn stops taping, no redeploy.

Resolution is user (users.data.diagnostics) > platform_settings > default-on, via
_as_flag/_resolve_capture_signal rather than _resolve_effective: a stored "false"
is exactly what a kill switch is for, and the truthiness fold would discard it and
fall through. An unrecognized value falls through instead of guessing (env_flag's
rule) — a typo is not an explicit opt-out.

capture_signal is ALWAYS present in the response. bot_spawn cannot distinguish an
omitted key from an unreachable identity, and both must default ON, so the edge
states it rather than leaving the caller to infer it.

feat(meeting-api): thread captureSignalEnabled into every spawn, default ON

The sealed invocation.v1 field already existed and the bot already honored it —
nothing ever set it. This wires the control plane: one best-effort bot-context
call now feeds two readers (the STT backend and the tape flag) instead of one,
so _resolve_transcription_backend becomes _fetch_bot_context + two pure readers.

Default ON is a failure-mode decision, not a config default. The lookup is
best-effort by contract, so an unreachable identity, a 500, an unset
ADMIN_API_URL, or an older admin-api that predates the field must all still
tape: only an explicit boolean false stops it. The alternative fails silently —
a transient identity blip turning collection off fleet-wide with prod looking
healthy and nobody noticing until the fixtures do not arrive.

The flag is orthogonal to recordingEnabled: a meeting nobody asked to record
still yields a fixture, and it rides the same recordingUploadUrl.

build_invocation strips None but not False, so the kill switch travels as an
explicit false rather than vanishing into the bot's env default — pinned by test,
because nothing else would notice the day that stops holding.

feat(meeting-api): store captured-signal tapes, and bound what we keep

Two halves of the same decision. Tapes ride the existing internal upload edge
(media_type=signal, jsonl) so no new endpoint, credential or network path is
opened from a bot — but they take a DIFFERENT server path, for three reasons:

  * no JSONB fold. Collection is default ON, so folding a tape into
    meeting.data['recordings'] would grow a phantom recording in every user's
    GET /recordings for every meeting they never asked to record;
  * no chunks, no master. The bot uploads one flushed file at teardown;
  * its own top-level signal/ keyspace, which is the janitor's constraint.

That last one is a deliberate correction to the recon's
recordings/{user}/{rec}/{session}/signal/ layout. The budget sweep must list
every tape in the bucket on a timer, and a nested layout would force it to page
through every recording chunk object in the deployment to find them. Top-level
keeps the sweep O(tapes). Key is signal/{user}/{meeting}/{session}/{part}.jsonl
— session-keyed because a tape exists for meetings that were never recorded, so
there is often no recording id to hang it off.

The keep-side budget is what makes default-ON safe: newest in, oldest unpromoted
out, until total tape bytes fit SIGNAL_TAPE_BUDGET_BYTES (50 GiB). A tape is
evicted whole (half a tape is not a smaller fixture, it is a broken one),
promoted tapes are never evicted, and when everything left is promoted the sweep
deletes NOTHING and says so — deleting the curated library to satisfy an
arithmetic target is a human's call, not a timer's. Anything younger than
SIGNAL_TAPE_MIN_AGE_S is skipped so a sweep firing mid-teardown cannot
half-delete a tape still arriving.

Storage grew list_detailed + delete: the sweep needs key+size+mtime, which S3
returns in the listing for free, and paying a head_object per tape on a timer
would be the wrong shape. delete is on the port rather than reached for through
the client so the blast radius is visible in the interface.

feat(teams): reopen the 0.10 closed-caption lane as a second attribution source

Teams delivers one server-side audio mix, so the WHO signal has to come from the
DOM. Today that is one source: the voice-level "blue-square" outline. This adds a
second, independent one — Teams' own live captions, which the platform's ASR
attributes to a named participant — and it is the same lane the 0.10 bot ran
before the 0.12 rewrite dropped it.

@vexa/teams-capture gains createTeamsCaptions: MutationObserver + 250 ms backup
poll (0.10 used 200 ms for the same reason — the virtualized caption list drops
mutations), pairing [data-tid="author"] with [data-tid="closed-caption-text"] by
DOCUMENT ORDER under [data-tid="closed-caption-renderer-wrapper"]. Those three
atoms are ported verbatim from v0.10.6/v0.10.7 (byte-identical across the tags),
where they were verified live on 2026-03-19 against BOTH host and guest views —
the host view interposes an items-renderer the guest lacks, so any structural
path between wrapper and atoms is host-only and rots. They are the same stable
data-tid family that survived the Fluent class-hash churn on the speaker side.

Teams refines each caption IN PLACE, so an entry is emitted on stabilization
(unchanged for 900 ms) or when a newer entry supersedes it — never per mutation.
An empty or non-name-shaped author WITHHOLDS the event and emits
caption-speaker-unresolved instead; the guard is isTeamsDisplayNameCandidate, now
exported so one place decides what may become a name.

CC is treated as flake-class, which is the point rather than a caveat: captions
are switched ON at join (the ported 0.10 More -> Captions / More -> Language and
speech menu path, bounded retries, VEXA_TEAMS_ENABLE_CAPTIONS=0 as a kill switch),
and every way that can fail is an observation, never an error —
captions-enable-failed, captions-active, captions-lost, captions-recovered,
captions-absent. Recovery is automatic. The outline watcher runs in parallel
throughout and is untouched by any caption outage.

Caption events cross to the Node side and go to the captured-signal tape and the
log — deliberately NOT to pipeline.recordHint. This iteration buys an observation
stream, not a behaviour change, and a caption that quietly became a naming hint
would rewrite speaker attribution while claiming to watch it. The tape write is
one optional sink method (captureCaption) the recorder does not implement yet, so
captions currently land on the log and light up the tape with no change here.

What the first live Teams meeting must confirm: that the caption renderer is
found at all. captions-active names the exact wrapper/author/text selectors that
matched; captions-absent carries per-candidate match counts, so a stale selector
and a captions-off meeting are distinguishable from one line.

Tests: 30 L2 checks over host + guest caption DOM, stabilization dedup, withheld
unresolved, absent-once, self-filter, teardown flush, and an outage that
recovers; plus a page->Node wiring test over the REAL browser bundle and the REAL
bridge that asserts captions reach the sink and never reach the name binder.
gate:isolation stays green (zero external imports).

feat(bot): cap the tape, carry every stream, and ship it at teardown

Three things a default-ON tape needs before it can run in prod.

CAP. Every prod meeting now writes into the pod's ephemeral storage. Unbounded,
one pathological meeting fills the disk — and a bot that dies of a full disk is a
lost MEETING, not a lost fixture. VEXA_CAPTURE_SIGNAL_MAX_BYTES (250 MB) stops
the tape and nothing else: no throw into capture, no leave, one typed
tape-capped observation rather than one per dropped frame. A garbled or empty cap
falls back to the default loudly — the v0.12.5 .env.example failure class, where
a set-but-empty line silently inverted a flag.

ALL STREAMS. captureCaption lands the Teams CC lane (249e2798) in the fixture,
because a replay with audio and outline hints but no captions cannot reproduce
the tie-break the live bot had. Captions go to a <session>.captions.jsonl SIDECAR,
not into the tape: captured-signal.v1 is SEALED at three records, the replay
loader validates line by line, and a fourth record type would stop every stored
session replaying the moment a Teams meeting produced a caption. Adding a
CaptionEvent to the contract is a v2 decision, not a side effect of wiring a lane.
Same precedent as the STT sidecar. Captions count against the same cap.

Writing the sidecar exposed a real defect while being tested: two fire-and-forget
appendFile calls complete out of order, which would scramble a stream whose whole
value is its sequence — and close() did not await them, so the teardown upload
would ship a truncated file. Appends are serialized and close() drains them.

SHIP. uploadSignalTapes runs after signalRecorder.close() (the file is finalized
there) and before the process exits, because the container's disk dies with it.
Best-effort by construction: it never throws and never rejects, so nothing in it
can revise the exit code the orchestrator already returned. ONE attempt — the
recording path retries because a lost chunk is a lost customer recording, but
retrying here burns the SIGTERM grace and risks turning a clean exit into a
SIGKILL, which costs the meeting the fixture exists to serve. Streamed, never
buffered (tapes are tens of MB, in a container already shutting down), with its
own 60s timeout. Oversized tapes are SKIPPED, not truncated: a truncated tape
reads as a complete one to a replay, which turns a missing fixture into a lying
one.

The transport is proven against a loopback http server rather than a mock, so the
multipart framing, the media_type=signal metadata and the timeout are tested as
shipped.

feat(mixed): suppress invented media-artifact text, and report every suppression

Whisper invents on non-speech, and this lane's windows are short, so it invents more than a
one-shot transcription does: on a 270s clean fixture the lane published six rows of
"Субтитры сделал DimaTorzok" / "Продолжение следует" / "Редактор субтитров …" that the same
audio transcribed straight through never produced. Those windows carry HEALTHY metrics
(no_speech_prob 0.0, avg_logprob -0.31) and their energy matches the speech around them — the
non-speech there is music, louder than the talking — so no confidence gate and no RMS floor
can see them. What identifies them is the string.

Measured against oracle-labelled rows from three replays (270s + 165s clean audio, and the
m24 Teams tape), caught / precision / real-rows-eaten:

  MIXED GATE (this change)   6   1.00   0        (hq)   0  —  0 (vg)   0  —  0 (m24)
  gmeet blocklist verbatim   5   1.00   0        (hq)   0  —  0 (vg)   2  0.50  1 (m24)
  duration floor < 1.0s     43   0.40  26        (hq)   4  0.50  2 (vg)  20  0.20 16 (m24)
  duration floor < 1.5s     56   0.30  39        (hq)   5  0.40  3 (vg)  30  0.20 24 (m24)
  repetition loop            0      —   0 anywhere

Duration floors are out: at their best they are 40% precise and eat 26 real rows, most of them
the short answers a meeting is made of. The gmeet lane's phrase list is reused for its matching
semantics but NOT verbatim — on m24 it deletes "Yeah." and "I don't know.", real speech from a
real meeting, which the gmeet lane can afford (per-channel, re-derivable) and this one cannot
(one mixed stream, nothing to re-derive from). hallucinations/mixed.txt is therefore the
media-artifact subset of those files, plus regexes for the credit-string family, which arrives
in endless variants; hallucinations-are-subset.test.ts pins the subset property and pins that
the eight known-risky phrases stay unadopted.

A suppression is never silent: the host gets a typed SuppressedSegment, the lane logs it, and
stats() counts it. VEXA_MIXED_HALLUCINATION_GATE=off disables it.

test(mixed): dump every publish call from the tape replay, drafts included

`--out-json` shows what SURVIVED; the retract question is what did not. Without the ordered
publish log there is no way to ask whether a word was ever shown to a viewer and then taken
away, which is exactly the charge against the retract leg.

With it, on m24: of the 119 oracle words missing from the final transcript, only 14 (1.7% of
the oracle) were ever published as a draft and never confirmed by their own turn or its
neighbours. The other 105 were never transcribed at all. The retract leg is not the leak.

fix(teams-capture): resolve speaker names structurally, not by obfuscated class

(cherry picked from commit 1cfa2c23ff7c7c67283ef64485e970f163edb374)

Verified: teams-capture suite 149 checks green (his 5 among them), check:isolation
clean, tsc clean.

feat(mixed): read the transport's own account of who is audible

The mixed lane receives ONE server-side mix, so nothing in the waveform says who is
speaking and the lane infers it twice — a segmenter guesses turn boundaries, a binder
guesses a name per turn from flickery DOM hints. But RTP already carries the answer:
the mixer stamps each packet with the CSRC list of the sources it mixed, and the UA
exposes the recent ones with a per-stream-stable id, a contribution timestamp and a
level.

createCsrcPoll is a SENSOR. It observes and emits transitions; it decides nothing,
names nobody, and reaches no pipeline. Three properties are deliberate, each against
the obvious alternative:

  - Transitions only. A 100ms poll over a steady speaker would emit ten identical
    records a second; steady state emits NOTHING.
  - Synthetic deactivation. The UA keeps listing a source for seconds after it stops,
    so presence in the latest poll is not liveness — the entry's own timestamp is. The
    deactivation edge is one the transport never sends, so we synthesize it.
  - Never throws into capture. One receiver whose getContributingSources throws is
    counted and skipped while the others keep working, and the first error emits one
    typed observation, not one per 100ms.

It reuses the remote-audio hook's peer-connection registry (new accessor,
observedPeerConnections) rather than patching RTCPeerConnection a second time: two
patches race, and the second wrapper would mirror every track twice — the doubling
webrtc-dedup.test.ts exists to prevent.

No platform vocabulary anywhere in the file; RTP mixing is a transport fact.

Implemented from the WebRTC specification (RTCRtpReceiver.getContributingSources);
no Elastic-licensed source consulted.

feat(bot): tape what the transport said, and what the bot noticed

Two new sidecars beside the captured-signal tape, and one reason for both: a replay
could reproduce what the bot HEARD but never what it NOTICED, so the question a
fixture is usually asked — "was the signal missing, or did we mis-read a signal that
was there?" — had no answer inside the fixture.

  <session>.csrc.jsonl          the transport sensor's turn edges (mixed lane)
  <session>.observations.jsonl  every typed observation the capture path emitted

Sidecars rather than tape records because captured-signal.v1 is SEALED at three
records and the replay loader validates line by line: a fourth record type inside the
tape would make every stored session fail its own contract the moment a mixed-lane
meeting observed a contributing source. Adding one is a v2 decision, not a side
effect of wiring a lane.

The observations stream is the bigger change of the two. signal-absent,
indicator-silent, captions-absent, main-audio-absent, captions-enable-failed,
csrc-poll-error — every one of them existed ONLY as a log line, in a pod deleted
minutes later. They are data now; the log lines are unchanged, this is additive. The
producer's payload is carried VERBATIM: a bridge that normalized it would be deciding
at capture time what a later analysis is allowed to see.

Also emitted as data rather than a log line: mix-topology, on the first mix and again
on every change. How many streams the mix is built from is a FACT about the meeting —
one server-side mix behaves nothing like N per-participant tracks, and the difference
decides how a tape may be read.

Mechanics that matter:

  - The three sidecars share ONE serialized-append implementation, and close() drains
    all of them. Bare fire-and-forget appends can land out of order, and a stream whose
    whole value is its sequence (an activation filed after its own deactivation
    describes a meeting that never happened) cannot survive that. The teardown upload
    reads these files the instant close() returns, so an un-awaited tail ships
    truncated — the same reason the caption reader flushes in the stop path.
  - Each sidecar's mini-header is written LAZILY, on the first record. A sidecar that
    never gets one must not exist at all: an empty-but-present file uploads as a
    fixture claiming a stream we never observed.
  - Everything counts against the ONE size cap. A 100ms sensor over a busy meeting can
    fill a disk exactly like a chatty audio stream.
  - The csrc poll's destroy() flushes a deactivation for every still-active source, so
    the meeting's last turn closes in the tape instead of dangling open.
  - NOTHING reads these records. __vexaCsrc is not wired to __vexaSpeakerHint; an
    observation that quietly became a hint would change speaker attribution while
    claiming to merely watch it. Asserted, not just stated: csrc-wiring.test.ts checks
    no transition and no observation reaches pipeline.recordHint.

image_version lands in the tape header and in every sidecar mini-header. A prod
fixture outlives the deployment that made it, and "the bot dropped the tail" means
opposite things on either side of a fix — without the build id a tape proves a
behaviour it cannot attribute. OPTIONAL and additive in the schema: the m24-era
goldens validate unchanged, which the contract gate confirms. 'unknown' is the honest
answer for an unstamped build, never a guess.

Implemented from the WebRTC specification (RTCRtpReceiver.getContributingSources);
no Elastic-licensed source consulted.

build(bot): stamp the build into the image, so a tape can name its own bot

VEXA_IMAGE_VERSION as a Dockerfile ARG→ENV, passed by every build path: the compose
`make bot` target and redeploy-bot.sh pass the short HEAD sha, the release workflow
passes the release version. telemetry.ts reads it into the tape header and every
sidecar mini-header.

An unstamped image records 'unknown' rather than guessing. A dirty tree still stamps
its HEAD sha — the tape says which commit, never which uncommitted edit, so a locally
built fixture is labelled approximately rather than falsely precisely.

feat(mixed): let the transport draw the turn, and name the track once

The mixed lane inferred twice: pyannote guessed where a turn began and ended,
and the binder guessed a name for each turn from tiles that flicker. Both
guesses have a measured cost — the segmenter's false negatives deleted 79 of an
oracle's 251 words, and the per-turn name race put one participant's speech
under the other's name for a whole meeting.

The RTP mixer already labels the mix it makes. So the turn edge becomes
something OBSERVED, and with it comes what pyannote could never supply: a
stable identity per speaker. The name question is then asked once per speaker
per meeting instead of once per turn, and only from spans where exactly one
source was audible while exactly one tile was lit. A track with no such
evidence publishes as "Speaker A" and stays there — unknown stays unknown.

Two voices in one mix cannot be cut apart, so concurrency opens a CONTESTED
turn that is published unattributed rather than handed to whichever source
happened to win. Both spines run all session; the transport takes over on its
first transition and hands back, mid-meeting, on silence or absence — the ring
is shared, so the switch costs a flag and a clean cut.

The pyannote lane is wrapped, not touched: every existing test scores the same
behaviour through the new seam.

feat(bot): hand the transport's edges to the lane, and the caption's author

A1 taped the transport transitions and stopped there, deliberately: nothing
read them, so no transcript could change. This is the hop it left out.

The mixed branch arms the spine as 'auto' rather than 'csrc'. A client that
does not mix server-side emits no contributing sources at all, and a spine with
nothing to say would produce an EMPTY transcript rather than a degraded one —
so pyannote carries the meeting until the transport speaks, and takes it back,
mid-meeting on the same ring, if the transport goes silent under continuing
speech. Which spine is running is written beside the tape as a typed
observation, because a transcript carries no trace of what produced it.

The caption AUTHOR crosses too — the name and the time, never the text, and
only once the entry has settled. Both stay out of recordHint: a csrc is an id
and a caption is not a turn, and either arriving as a naming hint would put the
per-turn window race back on the one path built without it.

The wiring tests keep their negative check and gain the positive one they were
missing, including that the lane and the sidecar stamp each edge identically —
without that a replay scores a run the live bot never had.

test(mixed): prove the spine cuts, the namer refuses, and the A/B is one flag

The replay harness could only ever score the naming path, because its turn
windows came from the live run. It now takes a --turn-source: the recorded
windows (the stable baseline), the REAL streaming segmenter (the only honest
way to score the fallback on a tape with no recorded windows), the transport
sidecar beside the tape, or auto. It also scores against the platform's own
captions, which makes a Teams tape carry its own attribution reference — no
third party, no hand-labelling.

"Speaker A" now scores as UNATTRIBUTED everywhere. It names a distinct person
we could not name, and counting it as a name would flatter every number in the
file.

The track-namer test replays the m30 SHAPE: two sources, and a DOM that named
exactly one of them all meeting. Because the tiles trail the audio by a second,
the other source accrues real-looking evidence for that same name — so a namer
taking each track's best candidate would confidently call BOTH tracks leo, out
of entirely correct data, and erase a participant. The check asserts the leak
happens and that the name still goes to one track only, so exclusivity cannot
be tuned away later by someone who has forgotten why it is there.

feat(bot): keep what the bot said, and what the meeting finally read like

Two questions a stored fixture could not answer. The tape says what the bot
HEARD and the observations say what it NOTICED, but neither says what it SAID
about its own run — the running commentary a human actually debugs from lived
only in a pod deleted minutes later, so every "why did it do that?" began by
asking for a log nobody still had. And the transcript a viewer was left with is
a FOLD over the publish stream (upsert by id, delete on retract) that every
consumer performs and nobody stored, so "what did this meeting say?" could only
be answered by re-running it against a redis that is gone by the time anyone
asks.

<session>.botlog.txt is the one deliberate exception to whole-or-absent. Every
other artefact is skipped rather than truncated because half a tape reads to a
replay exactly like a complete one — a missing fixture becomes a lying one. A
log is not replay input: a human reads it, and a human reading "N bytes of log
dropped here" is not misled. So a long meeting keeps its head and its tail and
names the gap between them.

<session>.transcript.jsonl is the snapshot, never the audit trail — the publish
stream is the audit trail. Both join the closed part set on both sides, and the
format is a property of the part rather than of the caller, so a bot cannot
upload a text file under a key whose extension claims it is JSON.

fix(mixed): replay the language the tape was recorded with, not 'en'

The harness hard-coded English. On the m30 fixture — a Russian conversation —
that made Whisper TRANSLATE the meeting, so the replayed transcript shared
almost no words with the original and every word-level comparison was measuring
the harness instead of the lane. The tape header already records what the live
bot was configured with, including 'nothing, let Whisper decide', which is what
that bot actually did.

feat(teams,mixed): read the roster, and name the last speaker by elimination

The founder's review of the m30 replay: separation green, transcription green,
attribution RED — "Speaker A" where his name belongs. He is right, and the
reason is structural rather than a tuning miss. Every naming path in this lane
answers "who is speaking now", which is a question about the voice-level
outline — and on m30 that outline named exactly ONE of the two participants for
the whole meeting. No amount of listening could have named the other. He was in
the roster the entire time.

So the producer now emits the roster as its own typed observation: who is in
the room, whether or not they can be heard. It walks every matched tile BEFORE
the signal gate, because a participant with no outline is invisible to every
other path in that file and is exactly who this is for. It goes through the
same display-name guard as every other name, excludes the bot, and stops
repeating after a few scans so an hour-long meeting does not write thousands of
identical lines into its own fixture.

A roster name is never a hint. It carries no time, so treating one as speaking
evidence would attribute a turn to somebody for merely being present. It does
two things: it supplies the casing Teams considers canonical, and it makes
elimination possible — when exactly ONE track is unnamed and exactly ONE roster
name is unclaimed, they are each other.

That rule is deliberately the strictest form of the argument. Two unnamed
tracks and it refuses; two unclaimed names and it refuses; a track already
named from evidence is never revisited, and a name reached this way is recorded
as 'elimination' so a reader can tell it from a measurement. Silence in a
three-and-three meeting is the correct answer, and the test that pins it is the
one to keep: a rule that paired anything there would be printing a human's name
off a coin toss.

Orphan spans get the same treatment from the other side: a span the transport
declined to own is checked for whether it was AMBIGUOUS or merely unowned, and
inherits a name only when exactly one track could possibly have been in it.

fix(mixed): take the elimination late, or it is a race wearing an argument

The first run of the roster rule named both m30 speakers correctly and marked
BOTH of them 'elimination' — including the track carrying 36.7 s of direct
evidence for its name. That gave the game away.

A roster fills one name at a time. Between the moment the first name finishes
corroborating and the moment the second appears, the set looks exactly like a
decidable one-track-one-name — so the rule fired on a transient, and only then
did the evidence path get to run. On this fixture it reached the right answer
for entirely the wrong reason, which is worse than reaching the wrong one:
nothing about the output said so.

Elimination is a last resort and must now be taken as one. The roster has to
have shown no new name for a settle window before any pairing counts, and the
rule is re-tested as time passes rather than only when a name arrives — because
once the room has settled, no further sighting is coming.

The test that pins it is the half-filled roster: one track, one fully
corroborated name, and the answer is still nothing.

fix(teams,mixed): a bot is not a speaker, and a placeholder is not a name

The live witness failed with a human's speech published under our own bot's
name, and other rows published as "Unknown user". Four doors were open, and the
fixture says which:

The self filter compared raw strings, so "Vexa (Unverified)" was not recognised
as the bot that joins as "Vexa" — it entered the roster as a participant, and
elimination then had exactly one track and one name left and handed a BOT'S
NAME TO A PERSON. Identity comparison now strips the qualifiers Teams appends
(Unverified/Guest/Bot, "Vexa 2"), for comparison only: the transcript still
renders whatever Teams rendered.

"Unknown user" is Teams saying it does not know who someone is, and it arrives
shaped exactly like a name — capitalised, spaced, through the same attributes.
It reached the transcript through the caption author. Placeholders (with locale
variants) are now refused at the same single guard every other name path uses.

Elimination itself needed two premises it never checked. A set containing a bot
or a placeholder cannot support "the only name left", because that is an
argument about people — one such entry now disables the rule for the meeting,
and the refusal is recorded rather than looking like an empty roster. And the
producer's scans saw FOUR tiles while resolving two names: a roster missing
people cannot support "the only one left" either, so the producer now reports
how much of the roster it could read and the rule refuses while that is short.

The meeting that produced this is unreachable, so the failure is manufactured
instead of awaited: an adversarial fixture carrying the polluted roster, the
placeholder captions, and the partial coverage, built from the extracted
evidence. It reproduces the defect and stays as a regression test.

perf(mixed): drive the replay from the tape's clock, not the wall

A replay had to run at 1x to be worth anything, because two things in the lane
are driven by the wall clock — the 1 s heartbeat that ticks, rolls and
TTL-finalizes the open turn, and the TTL's own comparison. Fired instantly, a
turn that lived through several growing submissions is transcribed in ONE, and
every defect that lives in the CADENCE simply does not occur. So every naming
iteration was paying eight minutes for a fact it did not need.

The tape already carries the timestamps. Injecting the clock lets the same code
paths run against the tape's own time: the m24 fixture replays in 12.6 s
instead of 478, and the m34 fixture in 2.8 s instead of 77. The lane's time
CONSTANTS are untouched — this changes what "now" means, not what the lane does
with it, and production still uses Date.now and setInterval.

The correctness argument is that the lane is asynchronous: a heartbeat enqueues
work a promise chain drains later, so the clock awaits that chain before moving
and fires each heartbeat at ITS OWN time rather than batching them at the
destination. A heartbeat that believes it is four seconds late makes different
decisions about a TTL, which is the class of defect this exists to reproduce.

Equivalence is proven, not asserted: on the adversarial fixture the virtual and
real-time runs produce identical durable rows AND an identical publish stream,
retractions included.

Two lane fixes the full m30 tape surfaced while proving it. Canonical casing is
now applied to every name the lane publishes rather than only on the track path
— the tiles render "leo" and the roster renders "Leo", and the transcript
carried one participant under both. And orphan containment now refuses when the
spine never reported a turn's membership: a TTL finalize can close a turn
before that report lands, and treating the silence as "nobody else was there"
named a 5.4-second crosstalk span after both speakers had talked through all
of it. Unknown is not empty.

test(mixed): make the virtual tier's equivalence claim checkable, and bound it

The equivalence holds exactly where the lane is deterministic and does not hold
where it is not, and the difference is worth writing down rather than averaging
away.

On the TRANSPORT spine every edge is derived synchronously from an event that
already happened, so virtual and real time produce byte-identical durable rows
and byte-identical publish streams — proven on the adversarial fixture and
pinned by a standing test that generates a small tape, runs it both ways, and
diffs drafts and retractions as well as the result.

On the PYANNOTE spine with the real ONNX model they do not, and the cause is in
the lane rather than the clock: appendFrame is fire-and-forget by design (the
capture path must never block on a model), so under a wall clock the inference
interleaves with the frames that arrive during it and the boundaries themselves
land differently. Measured on m24: 64 of 130 rows identical, and the segmenter's
own window signatures differ, which is upstream of anything the clock touches.
Virtual time is self-identical across runs on that same tape (128 rows, 253
publish calls, twice) — so it is the REPRODUCIBLE one, and the real-time run is
the run that cannot be repeated even against itself.

Sources can now report when they are settled, which the replay driver awaits so
that "let the lane catch up" includes the model. Production never calls it.

fix(mixed): a name another track already earned is contamination, not disagreement

The real m34 tape — recovered whole, 638 s, replayed in 11.8 s — showed both
name-hygiene doors holding: the bot was refused entry to the roster and the
platform's placeholder never became a speaker. But one of the two humans was
still published as "Speaker A" for the entire meeting while carrying 10.4 s of
unambiguous evidence for his own name.

He was blocked by 7.1 s of evidence for the OTHER participant, which his track
accrued only because the tiles trail the audio by about a second — the exact
bleed this file's exclusivity rule exists to catch, and which the other track
had already settled outright with 82.8 s. His share came to 0.59, under the
bar, so the rule vetoed a name he plainly holds using evidence we had already
concluded belongs to somebody else.

Once a name is owned by another track it is a known contaminant, so it leaves
the denominator. This is not a loosened bar: the discount only removes names
another track earned under the full rules, and the winner still clears
corroboration, the same share, and the majority of its own name across all
tracks. Settling a name now also re-tests the other tracks, since it can free
their evidence.

Both humans on the real tape are now named FROM EVIDENCE — no elimination
needed, which is the better outcome: the last-resort rule stays unused wherever
the meeting actually said who was speaking.

fix(mixed): attribute at word granularity, not per turn

The founder challenged "12 unattributed = crosstalk" by pointing at one row —
a clean single-voice sentence published as "Speaker" — and he was right. The
audit says so plainly: of the 12, ELEVEN are spans where the DOM tiles named
exactly one person, and two sources are genuinely audible together for only
5.0% of the meeting, in stretches whose median length is one second. A whole
sentence is never that.

Two things were wrong. Attribution stopped at the TURN, so a turn the transport
could not assign took a whole sentence down with it. And the transport's "both
audible" was treated as the end of the inquiry, when the tiles are a second,
independent opinion about which of those two was speaking.

Whisper already returns word timestamps — the client has requested them all
along and nothing read them. Now each word is asked who owned its instant, and
consecutive words with the same answer stay together, so a turn may publish
under more than one name: the honest shape when the transport changes hands
mid-sentence. A word in a contested stretch is offered to the tiles, and takes
a name only when they name exactly ONE person AND that person already owns one
of the two tracks in the mix — the constraint that keeps this from becoming the
per-turn DOM race this lane was built to end.

"Speaker" survives, but as a sliver rather than a sentence.

fix(mixed): join word tokens verbatim, not with invented spaces

Whisper's word tokens carry their own leading space, and a suffix like "-то"
carries none precisely because it must not have one. Re-joining trimmed tokens
with a space put "что -то" into the founder's transcript. The decoder already
knows where the spaces belong; trimming now happens only at a piece's outer
edges.

feat(teams): read the roster panel, and say so when nothing can name anyone

Meeting 37 shipped an entire conversation as "Speaker A" and nothing in the run
said why. Three independent name sources were dark at once: the page had
degraded to ONE participant tile with no voice outline, the tile-based roster
walk therefore resolved nothing, and the caption lane had failed on the Teams
side. Refusing to guess was correct. Refusing to guess SILENTLY was not — an
anonymous transcript and a broken one look identical to whoever reads it.

Two additions. The roster PANEL is read as a second DOM surface, separate from
the tiles and with a different lifecycle, so a gallery layout that drops tiles
no longer takes naming down with it. It never OPENS the panel: clicking the
roster button changes what the humans in the meeting see, and the ruling now
retiring the captions lane applies here too — the bot reads the page, it does
not operate it. A closed panel yields nothing, which is honest.

And when no tile can hint and no surface has yielded a name while tiles exist,
that is now a typed `name-sources-absent` observation carrying the counts that
diagnose it — the same counts that took a live comparison against another
meeting to establish this time.

The panel feeds the same name stream and therefore the same single guard: a
placeholder or our own bot is refused there exactly as on a tile.

feat(teams): stop switching captions on in other people's meetings

Enabling captions meant the bot clicking through the meeting's own UI —
changing what the humans in the room see — to obtain a name source. The trade
is no longer worth making, because it was measured and the source is redundant.

Replaying m30, m34 and m36 with caption evidence WITHHELD produced byte-
identical naming on all three: m34's per-track evidence is 7132/10372/82831 ms
either way, m36's is 46923 ms either way, and every track captions helped name
was already named by the DOM tiles and the roster. wrong=0 and junk=0 held
throughout. The lane was paying a visible intrusion into somebody's meeting for
nothing.

The code path is kept, unchanged, behind VEXA_TEAMS_ENABLE_CAPTIONS=1. It is a
genuinely independent second attribution source and is worth having for a
tenant whose outline never renders. What it may no longer do is switch itself
on by default. A meeting that already has captions running is unaffected — this
governs whether the BOT enables them, not whether the reader consumes them.

The replay harness gains --no-captions, which withholds captions as name
EVIDENCE while keeping them as the scoring ORACLE, so the question "could this
have been named without touching the meeting?" stays checkable against the
reference that answers it.

feat(mixed): extract the source→name correlator, platform-agnostic

The same problem wears different clothes in two lanes: an RTP CSRC and a lit
Teams tile, an SSRC and a glowing Meet tile. One signal knows WHEN precisely
and nothing about WHO; the other knows WHO and is vague and late about WHEN.
This takes intervals and returns bindings, and mentions no platform.

Three properties, each forced by a real tape rather than chosen:

The lag is SCANNED per meeting, not inherited. Measured over the same code and
three tapes it is +1250 ms on two and +2000 ms on the third, against the
+1000 ms hard-coded from the first — a correlator carrying one meeting's
constant will quietly mis-bind another's.

Cross-source exclusivity is a HARD constraint, not a tie-break. On m30 the raw
co-activity picks the SAME name for both sources (67.8 s against 208.6 s),
because one tile stays lit through the handoffs. Letting each source take its
own best answer would name two people identically and erase one of them, so
pairs are ranked globally and a name goes to the source holding the clear
majority of THAT NAME's evidence.

And there is a margin, with silence below it — m34's thin case is 13 points.
Under the bar the correlator returns nothing and says which bar refused it.

`weight` is carried for the audio LEVEL that RTP reports per contributing
source and that none of these tapes contain: it scales co-activity and defaults
to 1, deliberately inert rather than speculatively tuned against data we do not
have yet.

fix(mixed): never re-transcribe audio that already produced a final, and cut long turns

Two defects a live single-speaker meeting surfaced, plus the label defect the
m36 tape exposed.

THE OVERLAP LEAK. The window advanced to the whisper SEGMENT's end, which is
routinely earlier than the audio that produced it, so after a pause the next
window re-fed the tail of already-final speech and Whisper re-emitted it as the
new row's prefix. Only DRAFTS can be retracted — a confirmed row is immutable —
so the duplicate published: on m36, "Есть какие-то реал-тайм глюнки." followed
by "Есть какие-то реал-тайм глюнки, но, в основном, …". One pause, one resume,
one sentence said twice. Word timestamps make the boundary exact, so the window
now advances past the last CONFIRMED WORD. A tail-dedup guard backs it up for
the case where a decoder reaches into the ring's context pad, bounded so a
genuine "да, да" survives: three tokens minimum, first segment only, and only
while the window starts close behind the confirmed boundary.

THE 9-SECOND WAIT. A continuous monologue produces no boundary, so its first
final waited for the speaker to pause. Past 4 s of unconfirmed audio the open
turn now rolls — everything so far confirms and a fresh turn continues on the
SAME track, so attribution is untouched and only the granularity of the finals
changes. TURN_MAX_MS stays what it was, a Whisper-window bound rather than a
latency control.

THE LABEL. Elimination could beat the evidence path to the punch, so m36's
track read [elimination] while holding 46.9 s of its own unambiguous evidence —
the audit trail understating its own confidence. Evidence now upgrades the
record in place. The NAME is never changed by this: an elimination already
published is not overturned by later evidence for a DIFFERENT name, it is
logged as the contradiction it is.

fix(teams): abandon a mainAudio mix that is present but carries no sound

Observed live on staging (meeting 25689, 0.12.22-rc.1): three remote audio
tracks mirrored, the mainAudio pick connected as the single capture stream,
and not one word ever reached the transcriber. No energy meant no pyannote
boundaries, so no turn ever opened, so every speaker hint arrived with
nothing to overlap (binder-matched=0, missed=96) and nothing was ever
submitted for transcription. Zero POSTs to the gateway for the meeting's
whole duration, from a bot that looked healthy in every log.

The absence fallback only ever asked whether a mainAudio track APPEARED. One
that appears and then stays silent answers yes forever. Worse, the lane's own
rescue could not fire either: the csrc watchdog demotes back to pyannote only
after CSRC_DEATH_MS of ENERGETIC audio, which silence never supplies — the
recovery path needs the very signal that is missing.

So meter the picked mix as it is captured and, if it has produced no audio
above the lane's own energy floor after VEXA_TEAMS_MAIN_AUDIO_SILENCE_MS
(20s), abandon it for every track. The verdict latches so the pick cannot
oscillate once the fallback's own audio arrives, but the report re-emits on
every rescan, like the absent case — a degraded capture must never look
healthy. Doubled words are recoverable; a silent meeting is not.

fix(mixed): export the silence verdict from the package, not just the file

The silent-mix fix (91a97792) added `mainAudioProvedSilent` to
teams-main-audio.ts and imported it in build-browser-utils.mjs, but never
re-exported it from the package barrel. The unit test passes — it imports the
file directly — while the bot's browser bundle resolves through
`mixed-capture-core/dist/index.js` and finds nothing:

  browser-utils-entry.js:14:2: ERROR: No matching export in
  "../../modules/mixed-capture-core/dist/index.js" for import
  "mainAudioProvedSilent"

That failed `build-bot` AND `build lite` on run 31525029895, so the silent-pick
fix has no image. A green file-level test is not evidence the package exports
what its consumers import.

Export the verdict, both thresholds, and the observation type alongside the
selector they belong to. Verified with the exact CI command
(`pnpm --filter "@vexa/bot..." run build`): the bundle now carries the symbol.

fix(mixed): a held source is not a second speaker

Staging meeting 25690 published eighteen multi-sentence rows as "Speaker" in
the middle of one man's continuous speech, with correctly named rows on both
sides of them. Not edge slivers — whole sentences, refused.

The tape says why. Both contributing sources read active across every one of
those spans, so the lane called them contested and refused. But both sources
are genuinely audible together for only 2% of that meeting, and those 2%
produced 22% of the rows. The second track is not a second speaker: it is the
mixer holding a source open. Its signature is in the run structure — 315 runs
at a median of 0.9 s for the man actually talking, against 31 runs reaching 39 s
for the man being carried, whose run starts thirty-odd seconds before a span and
continues past it.

Asking whether a tile was LIT could not separate them, because a lit interval is
mostly the absence of an end event: it is extended by grace and it survives
silence, so both tiles read lit throughout. Asking which tile is being
RE-ASSERTED does separate them. A hint event fires when the watcher sees the
outline move, and a speaker re-emits one every couple of seconds while a held
source emits nothing — 1308 events against 97 across that call. On the eighteen
refused spans a strict majority within a second either side decides seventeen,
sixteen of them to the speaker the founder identified.

It applies ONLY where the transport already said contested, so a single-source
row is never overridden by a tile, and a genuine tie still resolves to nobody.

fix(mixed): the tiles only get a vote if they can testify about everyone in the mix

The re-assertion tie-break resolved the staging meeting's held-source spans, and
then put NINE wrong names into m30 the first time it ran there. m30's outline
lights for exactly one of the two participants for the entire meeting, so a tile
majority in that room says "leo" no matter who is speaking — one-sided by
construction. Reading the other man's silence as absence is the same fabrication
this lane exists to refuse, arriving through a new door.

So the tiles may rule on a contested span only when they have testified about
EVERY source audible in it: each contesting track's owner needs re-assertions
somewhere in the meeting before their absence at an instant means anything. A
signal that has never once named someone cannot be evidence that they are not
the one talking.

Also: a segment with no word timestamps now asks who owned its span rather than
falling back to the turn's name. Without that, a decoder returning no words
could never resolve a contested span at all — every one would publish as
"Speaker" however clearly the tiles said who was speaking.

The guard costs coverage where it protects correctness: m34 returns to 21
refusals from 4, because early contested spans are adjudicated before their
tracks have earned names. m30 returns to wrong=0. That is the right way round.

feat(bot): publish nothing where we could not name the speaker

Founder ruling from the rc.3 witness call: a row labelled "Speaker" advertises a
failed claim. It is the product telling the customer, inside the customer's own
transcript, that it tried to identify someone and missed. A blank reads as a
continuation of the passage and costs the reader nothing.

So the three internal spellings of a refusal — the provisional segmentation id,
the "Speaker" placeholder, and the stable letter a distinct-but-unnamed
transport track carries — all publish as an empty speaker. Both lanes: the gmeet
placeholder reaches the same dashboard and gets the same treatment.

The refusal is not hidden, it is re-addressed. `speaker_key` still carries the
track identity, so a late attribution repaints exactly as before, and WHY the
lane refused is in the observations sidecar beside the tape. What ends is the
failure being addressed to the customer.

The mapping lives in ONE place, at the bot's publish boundary. The lane keeps
its internal labels, so the replay harness and every score built on it keep
counting refusals rather than going blind the moment the display string changed.

Verified against the DEPLOYED dashboard bundle rather than a local clone: it
groups consecutive rows by `speaker || ""`, so an empty speaker starts its own
block and can never be absorbed into the previous speaker's name block — the
silent-misattribution risk that would have made this worse than "Speaker". It
also carries no fallback label, so the blank renders blank rather than as
"Unknown".

fix(release): bound the gh buffer so the release gates survive a large batch (#1139)

release-value-gate and release-witness-script both shell out through an
execSync helper with no maxBuffer, so Node's 1 MB default applied. A release
compare carries every file patch, so the payload scales with the size of the
batch rather than with the few fields these scripts actually read:
v0.12.18...v0.12.22 returns 1,581,885 bytes across 77 commits and 242 files.

Both scripts therefore died with `spawnSync /bin/sh ENOBUFS` — the witness
receipt for that release could not be generated at all, and the value gate
reported "could not evaluate" instead of a verdict. The failure mode is the
wrong way round: the gates go blind on exactly the largest releases, which are
the ones most worth gating.

No verdict logic changes. Same requests, same parsing, same exit codes; only
the buffer bound moves. Verified against v0.12.22: the value gate now returns a
real verdict (23 of 23 PRs accepted, 54 unaccounted commits reported) and the
witness generator emits its 23 values instead of throwing.

Three sibling scripts carry the identical helper and the same latent defect —
scripts/docs-current-gate.mjs, scripts/merge-card-gate.mjs and
scripts/release-witness-template.mjs. They are left alone here to keep this
change to the two scripts that are currently blocking a release; they are worth
the same one-line fix before their payloads grow.

* fix(teams): hold edge indicators as levels — the hint path was dead

and no SPEAKER_START log line at all. Diagnostics alive, hint path dead — Teams

and again in headless Chromium after.

ROOT CAUSE. Candidates come in two shapes and I conflated them. vdi-occlusion
and aria-state are LEVELS: they answer "is this tile speaking right now" on any
sample. inline-style-motion and class-token-delta are EDGES: they answer "did
something just change", which is true on exactly the one sample that observes
the change and false on every sample in between. Speaking is a level. With rAF
sampling at ~60fps and a voice bar updating every ~150ms, an edge read raw is
true on 1 sample in 9, so the level flapped at the sampling rate. The 200ms
hysteresis then admitted an alternating transition roughly every 200ms, and
because the 300ms debounce is LONGER than 200ms, each pending emit was cancelled
by the opposite transition before it could fire. Proved by construction: with
debounceMs=0 the same run yields 3 START/END pairs instead of none.

FIX. A candidate now declares kind: 'level' | 'edge'; an edge is held for
indicatorHoldMs (default 400ms, comfortably above the gap between two voice-bar
updates) and read as a level. A continuously animating outline is then speaking
on EVERY sample: one admitted transition, one START; when the animation stops
the hold expires and one END follows. Verified in headless Chromium over the
real bundle and the real bridge: transitions=1, one SPEAKER_START edge, one
SPEAKER_END edge.

On the coordinator's suspects, honestly: the debounce-reset suspect was right
and is the proximate mechanism. The hysteresis suspect was wrong in its details
— silent->speaking was not rejected, it was ADMITTED three times, which is why
indicator-fired fired three times. The >=3-signature floor was not the cause;
it gates only the first two changes and removing it fixes nothing. And
indicator-fired is emitted from the same code path that schedules the emit, two
statements apart, so that suspect was wrong too.

exactly ONE sample per DOM change, so it never produced the between-updates
samples where the level collapsed. Two things close it:

    real timers, a real 16ms frame interval and the real 300ms debounce; with
    the hold reverted it reproduces the production symptom exactly (HINTS [],

    headless Chromium through the real startCaptureBridge, asserting one START
    edge and one END edge for an animating tile and zero hints for a tile with
    no outline. Green-or-skip where chromium is absent, same shape as
    capture-bridge.boundary.test.ts. With the hold reverted it goes red on
    transitions=3 and zero SPEAKER_START edges.

* feat(meeting-api): store captured-signal tapes, and bound what we keep

Two halves of the same decision. Tapes ride the existing internal upload edge
(media_type=signal, jsonl) so no new endpoint, credential or network path is
opened from a bot — but they take a DIFFERENT server path, for three reasons:

  * no JSONB fold. Collection is default ON, so folding a tape into
    meeting.data['recordings'] would grow a phantom recording in every user's
    GET /recordings for every meeting they never asked to record;
  * no chunks, no master. The bot uploads one flushed file at teardown;
  * its own top-level signal/ keyspace, which is the janitor's constraint.

That last one is a deliberate correction to the recon's
recordings/{user}/{rec}/{session}/signal/ layout. The budget sweep must list
every tape in the bucket on a timer, and a nested layout would force it to page
through every recording chunk object in the deployment to find them. Top-level
keeps the sweep O(tapes). Key is signal/{user}/{meeting}/{session}/{part}.jsonl
— session-keyed because a tape exists for meetings that were never recorded, so
there is often no recording id to hang it off.

The keep-side budget is what makes default-ON safe: newest in, oldest unpromoted
out, until total tape bytes fit SIGNAL_TAPE_BUDGET_BYTES (50 GiB). A tape is
evicted whole (half a tape is not a smaller fixture, it is a broken one),
promoted tapes are never evicted, and when everything left is promoted the sweep
deletes NOTHING and says so — deleting the curated library to satisfy an
arithmetic target is a human's call, not a timer's. Anything younger than
SIGNAL_TAPE_MIN_AGE_S is skipped so a sweep firing mid-teardown cannot
half-delete a tape still arriving.

Storage grew list_detailed + delete: the sweep needs key+size+mtime, which S3
returns in the listing for free, and paying a head_object per tape on a timer
would be the wrong shape. delete is on the port rather than reached for through
the client so the blast radius is visible in the interface.

* feat(mixed): read the transport's own account of who is audible

The mixed lane receives ONE server-side mix, so nothing in the waveform says who is
speaking and the lane infers it twice — a segmenter guesses turn boundaries, a binder
guesses a name per turn from flickery DOM hints. But RTP already carries the answer:
the mixer stamps each packet with the CSRC list of the sources it mixed, and the UA
exposes the recent ones with a per-stream-stable id, a contribution timestamp and a
level.

createCsrcPoll is a SENSOR. It observes and emits transitions; it decides nothing,
names nobody, and reaches no pipeline. Three properties are deliberate, each against
the obvious alternative:

  - Transitions only. A 100ms poll over a steady speaker would emit ten identical
    records a second; steady state emits NOTHING.
  - Synthetic deactivation. The UA keeps listing a source for seconds after it stops,
    so presence in the latest poll is not liveness — the entry's own timestamp is. The
    deactivation edge is one the transport never sends, so we synthesize it.
  - Never throws into capture. One receiver whose getContributingSources throws is
    counted and skipped while the others keep working, and the first error emits one
    typed observation, not one per 100ms.

It reuses the remote-audio hook's peer-connection registry (new accessor,
observedPeerConnections) rather than patching RTCPeerConnection a second time: two
patches race, and the second wrapper would mirror every track twice — the doubling
webrtc-dedup.test.ts exists to prevent.

No platform vocabulary anywhere in the file; RTP mixing is a transport fact.

Implemented from the WebRTC specification (RTCRtpReceiver.getContributingSources);
no Elastic-licensed source consulted.

* feat(bot): tape what the transport said, and what the bot noticed

Two new sidecars beside the captured-signal tape, and one reason for both: a replay
could reproduce what the bot HEARD but never what it NOTICED, so the question a
fixture is usually asked — "was the signal missing, or did we mis-read a signal that
was there?" — had no answer inside the fixture.

  <session>.csrc.jsonl          the transport sensor's turn edges (mixed lane)
  <session>.observations.jsonl  every typed observation the capture path emitted

Sidecars rather than tape records because captured-signal.v1 is SEALED at three
records and the replay loader validates line by line: a fourth record type inside the
tape would make every stored session fail its own contract the moment a mixed-lane
meeting observed a contributing source. Adding one is a v2 decision, not a side
effect of wiring a lane.

The observations stream is the bigger change of the two. signal-absent,
indicator-silent, captions-absent, main-audio-absent, captions-enable-failed,
csrc-poll-error — every one of them existed ONLY as a log line, in a pod deleted
minutes later. They are data now; the log lines are unchanged, this is additive. The
producer's payload is carried VERBATIM: a bridge that normalized it would be deciding
at capture time what a later analysis is allowed to see.

Also emitted as data rather than a log line: mix-topology, on the first mix and again
on every change. How many streams the mix is built from is a FACT about the meeting —
one server-side mix behaves nothing like N per-participant tracks, and the difference
decides how a tape may be read.

Mechanics that matter:

  - The three sidecars share ONE serialized-append implementation, and close() drains
    all of them. Bare fire-and-forget appends can land out of order, and a stream whose
    whole value is its sequence (an activation filed after its own deactivation
    describes a meeting that never happened) cannot survive that. The teardown upload
    reads these files the instant close() returns, so an un-awaited tail ships
    truncated — the same reason the caption reader flushes in the stop path.
  - Each sidecar's mini-header is written LAZILY, on the first record. A sidecar that
    never gets one must not exist at all: an empty-but-present file uploads as a
    fixture claiming a stream we never observed.
  - Everything counts against the ONE size cap. A 100ms sensor over a busy meeting can
    fill a disk exactly like a chatty audio stream.
  - The csrc poll's destroy() flushes a deactivation for every still-active source, so
    the meeting's last turn closes in the tape instead of dangling open.
  - NOTHING reads these records. __vexaCsrc is not wired to __vexaSpeakerHint; an
    observation that quietly became a hint would change speaker attribution while
    claiming to merely watch it. Asserted, not just stated: csrc-wiring.test.ts checks
    no transition and no observation reaches pipeline.recordHint.

image_version lands in the tape header and in every sidecar mini-header. A prod
fixture outlives the deployment that made it, and "the bot dropped the tail" means
opposite things on either side of a fix — without the build id a tape proves a
behaviour it cannot attribute. OPTIONAL and additive in the schema: the m24-era
goldens validate unchanged, which the contract gate confirms. 'unknown' is the honest
answer for an unstamped build, never a guess.

fix(identity): fail closed when a UNIQUE index cannot be created

schema-sync's additive index loop caught every CREATE INDEX failure and
continued — WARNING for unique, DEBUG otherwise. A non-unique index is a
performance hint, so tolerating it is correct. A UNIQUE index is an
invariant the application relies on, and tolerating that one produced a
silent, permanent lie.

Verified in production 2026-08-17: uq_meeting_active_user_platform_native
— the DB backstop meeting-api's bot_spawn/adapters.py documents relying on
— had NEVER existed. Four stale duplicate rows blocked it, every restart
re-attempted and re-swallowed the failure, and the lone WARNING
log-rotated away inside a day. The backstop was decorative the whole time
while admin-api reported itself healthy.

Unique-index failures are now collected across the whole pass and raised
as SchemaInvariantError, naming each index, its table, the underlying
Postgres error, and the remediation. The raise propagates out of
ensure_schema through admin-api's ASGI startup hook: uvicorn aborts
startup and exits(3), so the port never binds, /health never answers, and
the compose healthcheck plus the k8s startup/readiness probes never pass.
A DB whose duplicate rows block a load-bearing unique index must not be
served by a process that assumes the index exists.

It is explicitly not retried — #901's bounded connect retry short-circuits
on SchemaInvariantError, because a data problem needs an operator, not a
backoff. SchemaInvariantError lives in a SQLAlchemy-free schema/errors.py
so __main__ stays importable in the offline gate venv.

raise, its message, the one-raise-lists-all behaviour, the still-tolerated
non-unique path, and the no-retry wiring;
test_meeting_active_unique_index_blocked_fails_closed (docker-gated)
reproduces the exact prod shape on real Postgres — drop the index, plant
duplicate active rows, re-converge, raise; resolve the duplicate,
