fix(namer): an evidence name stays revisable until the roster settles

A track accepted a name from evidence measured against a roster that had not
finished discovering the room, and the acceptance was permanent. On production
meeting 26424 csrc:201 became "Matt" at +35s on 3.8s of evidence while the
roster held only "Matt"; the second participant's first roster sighting was ten
seconds away. 93.2% contrary evidence over the following 28 minutes could not
revise it, and exclusivity then correctly refused "Matt" to the track that was
Matt — one human's whole side of the meeting printed under the other's name.

TRACK_NAME_ROSTER_SETTLE_MS gated only the elimination path. It would not have
caught this even if applied to acceptance: the roster had been QUIET for 35
seconds and coverage called itself complete at 1-of-1. The one contradiction
available at that instant is that the transport was already carrying two humans
while the roster listed one.

So `rosterSettled` is quiet AND not-provably-behind, and an evidence name
earned against an unsettled roster is published at once but re-derived on every
evaluation until the roster settles: it may change, or be withdrawn and the
name released to the track that owns it. Past settle it is permanent exactly as
before. Elimination gains the same not-provably-behind test and is otherwise
untouched; a meeting whose roster never reports is settled by definition.

gateway: enforce API-key scope per route, deny by default

The rc.18 documented-API sweep against staging found a key holding ONLY the
`browser` scope answering 201 on POST /bots — and it really did schedule a bot
container (mtg-26362-7c9e8908), which it then stopped with DELETE. Same on
GET /bots, /bots/status, /bots/{p}/{n}/chat, /user/webhook and /user/calendar,
while /meetings, /transcripts/* and /recordings refused it correctly.

Two holes, one per family, and the second is the one that will recur:

  * /bots was declared {"bot", "browser"}, so `browser` alone satisfied it. The
    scope you would hand a lower-trust surface was a full bot-control credential.
  * /user/* had no declaration at all, and ROUTE_SCOPES was a PREFIX map whose
    misses returned None — which the caller read as "no scope required" and
    forwarded. Absence of a declaration meant absence of a check, so every route
    added since has been open by default and nobody had to decide anything.

So the table is now keyed by (method, route template) and is EXHAUSTIVE over the
router, and a miss DENIES:

  bot        anything that can make a bot exist, stop existing, or change how it
             behaves — the whole /bots surface, and the calendar connections,
             because an auto-join feed spawns bots through a different door.
  tx         the transcript / meeting-record plane (unchanged).
  bot or tx  recordings (unchanged), webhook config + deliveries, model and
             transcription prefs, /agent/*, /mcp — account-level surfaces where
             neither service scope outranks the other, but holding NEITHER is
             disqualifying.
  browser    reaches no route. v0.12 serves no browser-tool surface at this edge,
             so a browser-only key authenticates and does nothing else.

Only /health and /auth/me carry no scope, and they say so out loud in
UNSCOPED_ROUTES rather than by omission — a browser-only key must still be able
to discover that it is a browser-only key.

Deny-by-default has two walls. At request time an undeclared route answers 403
instead of forwarding. At BUILD time create_app raises if any registered route
declares nothing, so an under-declared gateway does not boot and the hole cannot
reach an image. Adding a route now requires deciding its scope; the check is not
an allowlist someone must remember to extend.

Only behaviour change for a key holding a real service scope: none. Every
provisioning path in the tree mints bot,tx (deploy/lite, compose harness, probe)
and the terminal mints bot,tx,browser. The one credential that loses power is
the browser-only key, which is the finding.

Per-RESOURCE authorization is untouched and still open on the agent domain —
this decides which KEYS reach a route, not which of the owner's objects they may
touch. The strict-xfail on GET /agent/meeting/stream still marks that gap.

Refs rc.18 sweep finding B2.

ci(release): a red release-images means the build failed, not that the map is unknowable

release-images concluded FAILURE on every successful rc freeze, by construction.
Verified identical on rc.14 (32066734685), rc.15 (32078414374), rc.16
(32095685040), rc.17 (32114472336) and rc.18 (32139430561): all twelve build and
publish jobs green, ten images on Docker Hub, and one red — `validate / resolve`
— which skipped every validation leg behind it.

The nested resolve leg pinned the sha256 of releases/vX/candidate-images.json.
That map records the digests the build has only just published, so at freeze time
its identity is not unreviewed, it is UNKNOWABLE. Adding an arm per rc reproduces
the failure on the next one; the ordering is inherent, so the gating has to move,
not the data.

Two checks now live in resolve and they are not the same check:

  floor     version-agnostic — every published manifest resolves and carries its
            required platforms. Unconditional. #949 replaced this check with the
            version-pinned map check, silently narrowing the floor to nothing for
            any version outside the table while the job header and delivery.mdx
            went on describing it. Restored verbatim.

  identity  the packet-bound candidate map. Enforced on every promote request,
            every stable version, and every version a committed map already names
            (identity knowable => it must be reviewed). Deferred in exactly one
            shape: prerelease AND promote:false AND no reviewed arm AND no map
            naming this version — the freeze window, and nothing else.

A deferral is announced, not swallowed: a ::notice, a line in the run summary, and
a rendered clause in guarantee line 1 driven by a new resolve output. A skip
nobody can see is the same defect as a red nobody can trust, inverted.

What stays fail-closed, unchanged: promote's own independent stable-promotion map
table, its release-promote Environment approval, its witness-gate and value-gate
needs, and release-images' alias-candidate digest-equality proof before any stable
tag is written.

The human bind/validate/freeze step was load-bearing on every rc and documented
nowhere — releases/README.md described a two-phase flow that does not exist
without it. Written down as § Bind, validate, freeze.

release/release-validate-gating.test.mjs lifts the decision block out of the YAML
and EXECUTES it under bash with the inputs Actions supplies, rather than matching
patterns a dead gate would still satisfy. Fifteen tests; three mutants checked red
(the original unconditional failure, an inverted promote guard, an `if:` on the
floor).

meeting-api: the meeting detail response ships only the fields it should

`meeting.data` is a shared row blob: alongside the meeting's own content it
carries operational state other parts of the system stamped there — the per-user
webhook config bot_spawn writes so the lifecycle callback can sign deliveries,
the transcript share grants and viewer roster, the authenticated-session path.
The read paths that ship `data` authorize owner OR transcript-share recipient OR
bound-workspace member, so "the owner put it there" is not a reason for a key to
ride the response.

Adds `project_response_data` next to the existing `project_calendar_sources` /
`project_list_data` in projection.py, and applies it on every response edge:
the transcript detail (`_merge_live_segments`, real store + fake), the meeting
detail (`GET /meetings/{id}`), the PATCH echo, and the list.

Deny-set rather than allow-list: `data` is an open multi-producer blob whose
light keys the detail view genuinely renders and which product work extends
continuously, so an allow-list would silently blank future fields — a data-loss
failure no test would catch. The deny-by-default property is recovered by
dropping credential-SHAPED key names (matched on whole key or _-suffixed tail,
so `token_count` is unaffected), and a test pins the set to the delivery path's
own `_INTERNAL_DATA_KEYS`.

The projection is a response transform and does not touch the stored row, so the
delivery path — which reads the signing config from `meeting_row["data"]` as
returned by `update_meeting_status`, not from any response — is unaffected. Two
tests cover that: one signs and verifies after a read has been served, one drives
the real WebhookSink end to end and verifies the receiver's check still passes.

meeting-api: make the response projection viewer-aware instead of blunt

#1243 closed a real cross-tenant disclosure — a transcript-share recipient was
served the OWNER's webhook_secret — but it closed it with one rule for every
reader, and that over-stripped. The v0.10 backward-compat suite went red:

  compat/v010_rest_compat_test.py::test_10_user_webhook_config_flow
  AssertionError: spawned meeting never carried webhook_url=… in data

That flow is SINGLE-USER: the same user configures a webhook, spawns a bot, and
reads their own meeting expecting data.webhook_url. So the v0.10 contract
promises an OWNER their own webhook config on their own meeting row, and the
unconditional strip broke it for everyone, not only for strangers.

The state in `data` is not one bucket. It splits by WHO may read it, so the
projection now splits with it:

  SENSITIVE_OMIT_KEYS — never shipped, to ANYONE including the owner:
    webhook_secret (+ webhook_secrets), share_grants (per-link secret_hash and
    allow-list), auth_userdata_path (S3 session material). Each has a dedicated
    endpoint; no meeting response is the right carrier. Credential-SHAPED key
    names (SENSITIVE_KEY_SUFFIXES) stay in this tier too — a key nobody has
    classified yet is withheld from the owner as well.

  OWNER_ONLY_KEYS — shipped to the OWNER, stripped for everyone else:
    webhook_url, webhook_events (the v0.10 contract), webhook_delivery/
    webhook_deliveries/outbound_events (the owner's delivery bookkeeping), and
    transcript_viewers — a share recipient must not be able to enumerate who
    else the meeting was shared with.

  RESPONSE_OMIT_KEYS is now the union: what a NON-owner's response drops. The
  pin against webhooks.delivery._INTERNAL_DATA_KEYS holds against it unchanged.

Ownership is threaded, never re-derived. Every edge had already computed it:

  * list (GET /meetings, /bots, /bots/status) — `_row` now computes is_owner
    ONCE and feeds both the api.v1 `shared` field and the projection's viewer
    tier, so the two can never disagree;
  * meeting detail (GET /meetings/{id}) — reads `shared` back off the row
    list_meetings already stamped (`is False`, so an absent value falls to the
    strict view);
  * transcript detail — get_transcript_by_id's authorization check already
    evaluates an owner branch; that same boolean is passed into
    _merge_live_segments / _transcript_doc. The native-keyed read constrains
    Meeting.user_id == user_id in SQL, so it passes True by construction;
  * PATCH echo — update_planned_meeting selects WHERE id = … AND user_id = …
    and returns None otherwise, so a non-owner never reaches the echo.

Both projections default viewer_is_owner=False: a caller that forgets to thread
the decision gets the STRICT view. The failure direction is a missing field,
never a disclosure.

The stored row is untouched, so the delivery path — which reads the signing
config from meeting_row["data"] at send time, not from any response — is
unaffected; #1243's two end-to-end signing tests are kept and still green.

Tests: 21 in test_response_secret_projection.py (was 12), covering the owner's
tier-2 keys present on all four edges, absent for a share recipient AND a
bound-workspace member on list + detail, tier 1 absent for everyone on every
edge, tier disjointness, and the strict default. Proven red in BOTH directions
against forced tiers: with #1243's unconditional strip 6 owner tests fail; with
a permissive always-owner view 6 non-owner tests fail.

meeting-api suite: 1154 passed, 5 skipped (baseline at this base: 1145/5).

* fix(identity): fail closed when a UNIQUE index cannot be created

schema-sync's additive index loop caught every CREATE INDEX failure and
continued — WARNING for unique, DEBUG otherwise. A non-unique index is a
performance hint, so tolerating it is correct. A UNIQUE index is an
invariant the application relies on, and tolerating that one produced a
silent, permanent lie.

Verified in production 2026-08-17: uq_meeting_active_user_platform_native
— the DB backstop meeting-api's bot_spawn/adapters.py documents relying on
— had NEVER existed. Four stale duplicate rows blocked it, every restart
re-attempted and re-swallowed the failure, and the lone WARNING
log-rotated away inside a day. The backstop was decorative the whole time
while admin-api reported itself healthy.

Unique-index failures are now collected across the whole pass and raised
as SchemaInvariantError, naming each index, its table, the underlying
Postgres error, and the remediation. The raise propagates out of
ensure_schema through admin-api's ASGI startup hook: uvicorn aborts
startup and exits(3), so the port never binds, /health never answers, and
the compose healthcheck plus the k8s startup/readiness probes never pass.
A DB whose duplicate rows block a load-bearing unique index must not be
served by a process that assumes the index exists.

It is explicitly not retried — #901's bounded connect retry short-circuits
on SchemaInvariantError, because a data problem needs an operator, not a
backoff. SchemaInvariantError lives in a SQLAlchemy-free schema/errors.py
so __main__ stays importable in the offline gate venv.

Tests: tests/test_schema_sync_fail_closed.py (non-docker) covers the
raise, its message, the one-raise-lists-all behaviour, the still-tolerated
non-unique path, and the no-retry wiring;
test_meeting_active_unique_index_blocked_fails_closed (docker-gated)
reproduces the exact prod shape on real Postgres — drop the index, plant
duplicate active rows, re-converge, raise; resolve the duplicate,
re-converge, index present and unique.

* fix(namer): an evidence name stays revisable until the roster settles

A track accepted a name from evidence measured against a roster that had not
finished discovering the room, and the acceptance was permanent. On production
meeting 26424 csrc:201 became "Matt" at +35s on 3.8s of evidence while the
roster held only "Matt"; the second participant's first roster sighting was ten
seconds away. 93.2% contrary evidence over the following 28 minutes could not
revise it, and exclusivity then correctly refused "Matt" to the track that was
Matt — one human's whole side of the meeting printed under the other's name.

TRACK_NAME_ROSTER_SETTLE_MS gated only the elimination path. It would not have
caught this even if applied to acceptance: the roster had been QUIET for 35
seconds and coverage called itself complete at 1-of-1. The one contradiction
available at that instant is that the transport was already carrying two humans
while the roster listed one.

So `rosterSettled` is quiet AND not-provably-behind, and an evidence name
earned against an unsettled roster is published at once but re-derived on every
evaluation until the roster settles: it may change, or be withdrawn and the
name released to the track that owns it. Past settle it is permanent exactly as
before. Elimination gains the same not-provably-behind test and is otherwise
untouched; a meeting whose roster never reports is settled by definition.

* gateway: enforce API-key scope per route, deny by default

The rc.18 documented-API sweep against staging found a key holding ONLY the
`browser` scope answering 201 on POST /bots — and it really did schedule a bot
container (mtg-26362-7c9e8908), which it then stopped with DELETE. Same on
GET /bots, /bots/status, /bots/{p}/{n}/chat, /user/webhook and /user/calendar,
while /meetings, /transcripts/* and /recordings refused it correctly.

Two holes, one per family, and the second is the one that will recur:

  * /bots was declared {"bot", "browser"}, so `browser` alone satisfied it. The
    scope you would hand a lower-trust surface was a full bot-control credential.
  * /user/* had no declaration at all, and ROUTE_SCOPES was a PREFIX map whose
    misses returned None — which the caller read as "no scope required" and
    forwarded. Absence of a declaration meant absence of a check, so every route
    added since has been open by default and nobody had to decide anything.

So the table is now keyed by (method, route template) and is EXHAUSTIVE over the
router, and a miss DENIES:

  bot        anything that can make a bot exist, stop existing, or change how it
             behaves — the whole /bots surface, and the calendar connections,
             because an auto-join feed spawns bots through a different door.
  tx         the transcript / meeting-record plane (unchanged).
  bot or tx  recordings (unchanged), webhook config + deliveries, model and
             transcription prefs, /agent/*, /mcp — account-level surfaces where
             neither service scope outranks the other, but holding NEITHER is
             disqualifying.
  browser    reaches no route. v0.12 serves no browser-tool surface at this edge,
             so a browser-only key authenticates and does nothing else.

Only /health and /auth/me carry no scope, and they say so out loud in
UNSCOPED_ROUTES rather than by omission — a browser-only key must still be able
to discover that it is a browser-only key.

Deny-by-default has two walls. At request time an undeclared route answers 403
instead of forwarding. At BUILD time create_app raises if any registered route
declares nothing, so an under-declared gateway does not boot and the hole cannot
reach an image. Adding a route now requires deciding its scope; the check is not
an allowlist someone must remember to extend.

Only behaviour change for a key holding a real service scope: none. Every
provisioning path in the tree mints bot,tx (deploy/lite, compose harness, probe)
and the terminal mints bot,tx,browser. The one credential that loses power is
the browser-only key, which is the finding.

Per-RESOURCE authorization is untouched and still open on the agent domain —
this decides which KEYS reach a route, not which of the owner's objects they may
touch. The strict-xfail on GET /agent/meeting/stream still marks that gap.

* meeting-api: the meeting detail response ships only the fields it should

`meeting.data` is a shared row blob: alongside the meeting's own content it
carries operational state other parts of the system stamped there — the per-user
webhook config bot_spawn writes so the lifecycle callback can sign deliveries,
the transcript share grants and viewer roster, the authenticated-session path.
The read paths that ship `data` authorize owner OR transcript-share recipient OR
bound-workspace member, so "the owner put it there" is not a reason for a key to
ride the response.

Adds `project_response_data` next to the existing `project_calendar_sources` /
`project_list_data` in projection.py, and applies it on every response edge:
the transcript detail (`_merge_live_segments`, real store + fake), the meeting
detail (`GET /meetings/{id}`), the PATCH echo, and the list.

Deny-set rather than allow-list: `data` is an open multi-producer blob whose
light keys the detail view genuinely renders and which product work extends
continuously, so an allow-list would silently blank future fields — a data-loss
failure no test would catch. The deny-by-default property is recovered by
dropping credential-SHAPED key names (matched on whole key or _-suffixed tail,
so `token_count` is unaffected), and a test pins the set to the delivery path's

delivery path — which reads the signing config from `meeting_row["data"]` as
returned by `update_meeting_status`, not from any response — is unaffected. Two

* meeting-api: make the response projection viewer-aware instead of blunt

#1243 closed a real cross-tenant disclosure — a transcript-share recipient was
served the OWNER's webhook_secret — but it closed it with one rule for every
reader, and that over-stripped. The v0.10 backward-compat suite went red:

  compat/v010_rest_compat_test.py::test_10_user_webhook_config_flow
  AssertionError: spawned meeting never carried webhook_url=… in data

That flow is SINGLE-USER: the same user configures a webhook, spawns a bot, and
reads their own meeting expecting data.webhook_url. So the v0.10 contract
promises an OWNER their own webhook config on their own meeting row, and the
unconditional strip broke it for everyone, not only for strangers.

The state in `data` is not one bucket. It splits by WHO may read it, so the
projection now splits with it:

  SENSITIVE_OMIT_KEYS — never shipped, to ANYONE including the owner:
    webhook_secret (+ webhook_secrets), share_grants (per-link secret_hash and
    allow-list), auth_userdata_path (S3 session material). Each has a dedicated
    endpoint; no meeting response is the right carrier. Credential-SHAPED key
    names (SENSITIVE_KEY_SUFFIXES) stay in this tier too — a key nobody has
    classified yet is withheld from the owner as well.

  OWNER_ONLY_KEYS — shipped to the OWNER, stripped for everyone else:
    webhook_url, webhook_events (the v0.10 contract), webhook_delivery/
    webhook_deliveries/outbound_events (the owner's delivery bookkeeping), and
    transcript_viewers — a share recipient must not be able to enumerate who
    else the meeting was shared with.

  RESPONSE_OMIT_KEYS is now the union: what a NON-owner's response drops. The
  pin against webhooks.delivery._INTERNAL_DATA_KEYS holds against it unchanged.

Ownership is threaded, never re-derived. Every edge had already computed it:

  * list (GET /meetings, /bots, /bots/status) — `_row` now computes is_owner
    ONCE and feeds both the api.v1 `shared` field and the projection's viewer
    tier, so the two can never disagree;
  * meeting detail (GET /meetings/{id}) — reads `shared` back off the row
    list_meetings already stamped (`is False`, so an absent value falls to the
    strict view);
  * transcript detail — get_transcript_by_id's authorization check already
    evaluates an owner branch; that same boolean is passed into
    _merge_live_segments / _transcript_doc. The native-keyed read constrains
    Meeting.user_id == user_id in SQL, so it passes True by construction;
  * PATCH echo — update_planned_meeting selects WHERE id = … AND user_id = …
    and returns None otherwise, so a non-owner never reaches the echo.

Both projections default viewer_is_owner=False: a caller that forgets to thread
the decision gets the STRICT view. The failure direction is a missing field,
never a disclosure.

The stored row is untouched, so the delivery path — which reads the signing
config from meeting_row["data"] at send time, not from any response — is
unaffected; #1243's two end-to-end signing tests are kept and still green.

* fix(meetings): converge a stuck 'stopping' meeting on stop_grace, not the untracked window

When Vexa is restarted while a bot is mid-leave, the 'stopping' row's workload becomes
untracked (the fresh runtime 404s the old, process-backend-dead worker). The untracked
escalation then waited the full untracked_grace (10 min) before failing it — and that
window is in-process, so it RESETS on every restart. Across a redeploy burst the row
never accumulated a full window and sat stuck 'stopping' (shown active in the UI)
indefinitely.

escalate its untracked workload on the short stop_grace instead of the long untracked
window. active/pre-active keep the conservative untracked_grace (a quiet-but-live bot
must not be reaped). Test proves stopping converges on stop_grace even with a long
untracked_grace.

* mcp: report_issue — let the calling agent tell us what broke

Every instrument in the loop reads; this is the one that writes back. A tenth
tool on the MCP surface so a coding agent mid-integration can file what it
tried, what happened, and which deployment shape — with meeting_id/platform as
the join key onto our own record of the same meeting.

Stateless and env-configured like the rest of the service: the ticket is POSTed
to VEXA_TICKET_SINK_URL (optional bearer VEXA_TICKET_SINK_TOKEN); unset means
the tool answers 503 "not configured" so a self-hoster gets a no-op, not a
crash. The sink receives a salted SHA-256 prefix of the caller's key as
caller_fingerprint — never the key itself. Text fields and logs are capped,
empty bodies rejected, and ticket text is forwarded as data, never interpreted.

fix(bot): deaf-leave guard — connected streams with zero frames never resolve left_alone (#1195)

The silence adapter's only oracle is frame arrival, so a bot whose capture chain
breaks mid-meeting (the #850 class, at 100% loss) hears nothing, lets the silence
window expire and leaves a LIVE meeting as `completed(left_alone)` — a recorded
success. The page already knows remote streams are connected and carrying data;
that bit never crossed the bridge.

- Carry stream presence page→Node as `__vexaStreamPresence(count)`, called from
  the mixed lane's existing 2s rescan. It counts the CONNECTED stream objects
  whose audio track is `live` and not `muted` — `__vexaMixSeen` cannot answer
  this (it is a monotonic id ledger, so it counts streams EVER connected, and a
  bot that once saw a participant could never resolve left_alone again).
- `RemoteAudioActivityTap.observeStreamPresence?(count)` (additive and OPTIONAL
  on both sides) plus frame ARRIVAL bookkeeping alongside presence: a zero-energy
  frame proves capture is alive without proving anyone is there. That split is
  the deaf/silent oracle.
- `deafCaptureGuardAdapter`: ready ∧ streams present ∧ no frame for the whole
  window ⇒ verdict `capture-fault` — left_alone is withheld, a loud structured
  line repeats every 60s, and ONE capture restart is spent. Holding is bounded by
  the orchestrator's existing maxActiveMs ceiling.

One predicate, two defects. #866 (PR #887, @Ayush7614) latches remote-audio ready
when the mix destination attaches rather than on the first PCM frame, so an empty
mixed-lane room can reach left_alone at all. That is the right fix at the point of
introduction, but on its own it also removes the accidental protection that a
never-started capture could never latch ready — making THIS defect fire more
readily. Neither change is safe alone. Stream presence is the bit that separates
them, so one predicate covers both: zero streams ⇒ empty room ⇒ leave (#866);
streams live but silent ⇒ deaf bot ⇒ hold (#1192). Two timelines simulate #887's
earlier latch directly and pin both outcomes, so this lands safely before or after
it. The guard touches no line inside the block #887 refactors.

Refs #844, #866, #850, #887.

fix(runtime): spawned Pods declare CPU/memory requests and limits (#1005) (#1093)

* fix(runtime): spawned Pods declare CPU/memory requests and limits (#1005)

A namespace whose policy requires every container to declare CPU and memory
requests AND limits rejected both workload classes the runtime creates
dynamically, so no meeting bot and no agent worker could start there. The
runtime.v1 contract already carried the intent — the kernel accepted
`WorkloadSpec.resources` and then dropped it before calling the backend.

Resource intent now crosses the Backend port. The kernel resolves the effective
sizing (the spec's own, else the profile's deployment default) and hands it to
`Backend.start`. The Kubernetes backend submits a COMPLETE Pod manifest via
`kubectl create -f -` instead of `kubectl run --overrides`: a partial
`containers` entry in an override is a JSON merge patch that replaces the
generated container wholesale, so the image, env and command vanish and the API
server answers `spec.containers[0].image: Required value`. Owning the object
makes the merge ours and deterministic — resources, workspace volumeMounts,
image, command, env, labels and scheduling all coexist on the same container.

runtime.v1 carries one value per dimension, so cpu and memoryMb set BOTH the
request and the limit (Guaranteed QoS); the sealed contract is untouched and no
separate request/limit semantics are invented. A GPU count maps to the limits
side only, as Kubernetes requires for an extended resource. Zero is treated as
unset, and a negative value now fails at parse time against the schema's floor.

The two classes are sized independently from the chart:
`runtime.workloadResources.meetingBot` and `.agentWorker`, rendered onto the
runtime as four env keys the k8s backend reads. Leaving a class empty emits no
resources at all, preserving the optional contract and the previous unsized
spawn. Enforcement is Kubernetes-only: the docker and process backends accept
the same intent without acting on it — they have no admission controller to
satisfy, and a memory ceiling introduced there would OOM-kill live bots that run
unbounded today. No parity is claimed.

fix(gates): report the failure instead of swallowing it (#1107) (#1114)

* fix(gates): report the failure instead of swallowing it (#1107)

Every gate in gates.mjs reported its own failures through

    (e.stdout || e.stderr || e).toString()

Under stdio: 'pipe' a child that writes only to stderr leaves e.stdout as a
ZERO-LENGTH Buffer. An empty Buffer is an object, so it is truthy, so the || chain
short-circuits on it and returns the empty string. The operator sees the gate's
name, a colon, and nothing:

    ▶ gates: schema
      ✗ schema core/agent/contracts/event.v1:

    ❌ gates failed
    ✗ pre-push: gate:schema FAILED — push aborted (fix it, or bypass with: --no-verify)

A gate that cannot say why it failed is worse than one that does not run: the only
remaining move is the --no-verify the hook itself suggests, which is exactly the
habit these hooks exist to prevent. Found when gate:schema aborted a docs-only push
and the message was blank; the underlying cause turned out to be a missing ajv in a
fresh worktree, invisible behind the empty string.

Replaces all 22 sites with one errText() helper that chooses on LENGTH rather than
truthiness, preferring stdout, falling back to stderr, then to the error itself.
The .slice() calls are preserved — the helper returns a string.

Test drives a REAL execSync failure rather than a hand-built object, because the bug
lives in what Node actually attaches to the thrown error; a fixture asserting against
{stdout: Buffer.alloc(0)} would pass against a wrong implementation checking != null.
It also asserts the precondition (empty Buffer is truthy) so the test still means
something if Node changes, and guards against the pattern returning anywhere.

Red-before/green-after: with the old expression 3 of 5 fail; with the fix, 5 of 5
pass. gate:readme, gate:schema and gate:exports all still green.

fix(transcription): stop a CPU worker admitting a GPU-sized concurrency default (#1156)

* fix(transcription): stop a CPU worker admitting a GPU-sized concurrency default

MAX_ACTIVE_REQUESTS defaulted to 20, a figure benchmarked on an RTX 4090. On a CPU device each of those 20 admitted jobs only gets 1/20th of the cores, so none finish in bounded time, the semaphore never releases, and with FAIL_FAST_WHEN_BUSY every later request 503s. The worker keeps answering /health with 200 the whole time and never self-recovers. Observed on a 12-core CPU deployment: 503 on every POST for hours, a 51-minute meeting force-completed as stt_degraded with zero transcript rows, cleared only by a container restart.

- default MAX_ACTIVE_REQUESTS is now device-aware: 20 only for an explicit cuda device, 2 otherwise. Inverted deliberately so faster-whisper's "auto" (which can resolve to CPU at runtime) does not inherit the GPU default. An operator-set env var still wins.
- DEVICE is normalized once at read time, so every comparison in the file tolerates casing and stray whitespace.
- bound the whole request with TRANSCRIPTION_TIMEOUT_S (120s) so a call that never returns cannot hold its semaphore permit forever. The bound covers all temperature-fallback attempts together, not each one.
- size the thread pool one larger than the semaphore. asyncio.wait_for can only reclaim the permit, not the thread, so without headroom the next admitted request just queues behind the zombie and the reclaimed permit buys nothing.
- warn at startup when the medium or large model family is paired with a CPU device. deploy/transcription/docker-compose.cpu.yml already documents medium as shedding load with 503 on CPU, and large-v3-turbo measures ~0.95x realtime there (a ~30s chunk takes ~29s), so neither sustains a live meeting at any concurrency. Prefix match, so distil-* models are not flagged alongside the family they were distilled from.
- add http_504 to the transcription LB's proxy_next_upstream list. The app can now return 504, and a wedged worker is the worst case to keep sending traffic to, so it must fail over like the 503s already did.

This closes the specific deadlock the incident hit (a GPU-sized default admitted on a CPU device) but only narrows the general one: a single native call that truly never returns still burns one thread forever, the pool never recycles it, and the executor's +1 headroom only absorbs one such zombie at a time, so N+1 cumulative hangs over the process lifetime (N = MAX_ACTIVE_REQUESTS) still exhaust the pool and reproduce the same symptom. Actually killing a hung call needs subprocess isolation, which is deliberately out of scope here.

fix(mixed): the virtual-time speed check measured the runner, not the tier (#1300)

`virtualMs < realMs` compared two numbers that scale differently. The 1x run's
wall clock is FLOORED by the tape (~8.5 s, ~2% variance across CI runs); the
virtual run is pure compute — and strictly MORE compute than the 1x run, because
every event and every heartbeat awaits a drain that `--realtime` never performs.
On a fast machine that costs ~1 s and the comparison looks comfortable; on a
2-core CI runner it stretches past the floor and the comparison inverts. It has
been red-lighting PRs whose entire diff is one Markdown file: 10035 vs 8672 ms on
#1288, and 14687 vs 8496 ms on an unrelated release recut.

Assert the mechanism rather than a side effect of it. VirtualClock gains
advancedMs(); tape-replay reports it beside the heartbeat count it already
printed; the test asserts (a) a heartbeat fired for every second of lane clock —
which the old check never tested at all, since a tier that fired NO heartbeats
would have been fast and passed — and (b) the run came in under the lane time it
replaced, the boundary a clock that genuinely slept cannot cross. realMs is still
measured and printed for reading failures; it is simply never asserted on.

* fix(bot): vote-based per-track speaker attribution (self-correcting, 1:1)

Per-track SEPARATES each Zoom speaker onto their own stable WebRTC stream (verified
live: 5 streams for 5 speakers, appearing as each first spoke, never remapped), but

loudest track to whatever the DOM said, so the flaky signal scrambled the names.

Replace it with a VOTING resolver that attaches each stable stream to a name and
defends it against the flaky DOM:
- VOTE: every clean moment (this channel is the loudest hot one + exactly one speaker
  lit) casts one channel↔name vote; the binding is the argmax. A wrong early sample
  is one vote the true speaker outweighs — SELF-CORRECTING, no bad first bind locks in.
- MARGIN hysteresis (3): a new leader must beat the current binding by MARGIN to flip,
  so stray sticky-DOM votes can't churn an established name.
- 1:1 BY IDENTITY: a name is another ACTIVE channel's identity and can't be stolen even
  if the sticky DOM over-votes it elsewhere. Frees up when its owner goes long-idle
  (IDLE_RELEASE_MS=8000) — so leave-then-rejoin under a new stream works. Exception:
  two genuinely same-named people each earn the name with HIGH-PURITY votes (0.7) → both
  named; a mixed minority (contamination) does not qualify.

* feat(meetings): typed join-failure evidence with an attribution axis (#1059, #1058)

Every hosted `join_failure` meeting carried `data.reason = None` — 83 of 83 —
and a ~20s Teams refusal shared its label with a ~13min Meet lobby expiry.

ROOT CAUSE of the empty reason: nobody failed to report it. The bot stamps a
human `reason` on every terminal it emits, the reconcile sweep stamps the
probe's own answer, and `MeetingRecord.reason` held it. It was never
PROJECTED: `MeetingRecord.data` wrote the reason only into
`last_error.reason` — a key the list view drops (`LIST_OMIT_KEYS`) and which
`data->>'reason'` cannot see. Hoisting it to the top level is the fix.

TAXONOMY (two independent axes, alongside the untouched sealed
`CompletionReason`, which stays the retry classifier's input):

  reason      platform_rejection · admission_timeout · auth_session_missing ·
              never_reached_lobby · navigation_failure ·
              stopped_before_admission · unknown
  attribution system_fault · user_action · host_action ·
              exogenous_platform · unknown

The attribution axis is what makes the reliability gate computable:
`system_failure_rate = failures(attribution=system_fault) / fair-chance
meetings`. A user who stopped their own bot and a host who never clicked
admit are funnel outcomes, not software failures.

The two conflated populations now separate on the timing signature: a lobby
exit that burned ≥90% of the budget WE issued is an expiry (host_action); one
well inside it with no denial is a refusal; a bot that never saw a lobby is
never_reached_lobby (system_fault).

EVIDENCE lands at `meeting.data.join_evidence` — typed reason, attribution,
stage, source, stage timings, and the platform's own signal (capped). The bot
classifies at the source (it holds the DOM verdict and the clock); meeting-api
validates that verdict and derives one when a producer sends none, so
reconcile-driven, runtime-destroy, and legacy-bot terminals are evidenced too.

FAIL-OPEN throughout: this describes a run that has already ended, and no
fault in producing it may alter the terminal being recorded. Proven, not
asserted — a driver whose evidence channel throws, and a monkeypatched
classifier that explodes, both leave the terminal, the exit code and the
callback's 200 unchanged.

Additive on lifecycle.v1 (`additionalProperties: true`), the same no-seal-bump
path `infra_fault`/`stt_fault` take. NO contract re-seal: the seal hashes only
`*.schema.json`, and api.v1's `MeetingResponse.data` is already open.

* F105 — gate:isolation reads import STATEMENTS, not the word "from" wherever it appears

Second occurrence in one day, same defect. The terminal brick's specifier scan was
`from\s+['"]…['"]` with no anchor, so it read the words `from "…"` as an import anywhere they
sat. In the morning it failed a whole push on three files whose "undeclared dependencies" were
`a link was clicked` and `this turn did not come from an arrival` — English, in doc comments, in
files about links. That was fixed by stripping comments. This evening it failed again on a
REGEX LITERAL, which is code, survives the comment strip, and was never the prose half of the
problem.

Both are one defect, and it is the expensive kind: the gate reported a real-looking violation,
with a file name and a specifier, and was wrong. A gate that contradicts observable state gets
read before it is obeyed.

A static import or re-export is a STATEMENT — it begins a line. The scan is now anchored there,
and the clause may span lines but can never cross a quote or a semicolon, so it cannot run out of
its own statement into the next one. Three forms, and the anchor is what separates the keyword
from the same six letters quoted inside an expression:

  1. `import … from "x"` / `export … from "x"`, multi-line `{ a, b }` clause included
  2. `import "x"` — the side-effect form, which the old regex did not see AT ALL
  3. `require("x")` wherever it sits, with a preceding-character guard

Deliberately not a form: a bare `import("x")`. In TypeScript those characters are also the
type-query — `Content: import("mdx/types").MDXContent` at ui-kit/MdxDoc.tsx:268 names a types
package that is never installed at runtime, and adding it as form 4 reported that line as an
undeclared dependency. Telling a type query from a dynamic import needs a parser; this is
deliberately not one, and no file in src/ loads a runtime module that way.

scripts/check-isolation.test.mjs pins all of it — 8 rows, run in CI by the gates.yml static job's
existing `node --test scripts/*.test.mjs` step. Fixtures are planted as REAL FILES in the tree
the gate walks and the REAL gate runs as a subprocess: feeding a fixture string to an exported
regex would prove the regex, not the gate, and the scan is the whole of what is under test. Four
negative controls (a real import, the side-effect form, and a multi-line clause must all still
RED, by name) sit beside the four green rows, so the fix cannot be a scan that sees nothing.

Reproduction: on the parent commit rows 5-8 fail — a string, a regex literal, a comment and a
type query each reported as an undeclared dependency; row 3 fails too, because the side-effect
form was invisible. The other 18 bricks carry their own copy of the old scan and are NOT touched
here: each has its own rule set, `gate:isolation` is green across all 19, and fanning one edit
across 18 files that nobody has seen fail is how a fix becomes a blast radius.

declared none of them, and FastAPI drops an undeclared query parameter in
silence. **An argument that is accepted and ignored is worse than one that is
refused** — the caller cannot tell the answer is not the one they asked for. So
the parameters are declared with bounds: out of range is now a 422, not a clamp.

because there is no recordings table — recordings live inside `meeting.data`

the natural order is oldest-first; the sort therefore happens at the route, on
`created_at`, which `_now_iso()` guarantees is lexicographically chronological.

`chunk_count`, `first_chunk_at` and the rest — how the bytes were assembled,
which nothing in a list renders and no caller can act on. The list row now keeps
id, meeting_id, status, created_at, completed_at, playback_url, a top-level
duration_seconds (the longest of its media files — a list wants to know how long
it is), and per media file only id, type, format, duration_seconds,
file_size_bytes. The id and type are kept deliberately: they are how a caller
reaches /media/{id}/raw. Full fidelity stays on GET /recordings/{id}.

Not changed, and out of scope: the read behind this still materializes the whole
account (the JSONB layout gives it no choice). What changes is the RESPONSE,
which is what reaches a caller.

stored pointer is never the zero-byte final-signal chunk now reads `storage_path`
